    /sys/bus/mdio_bus/devices/ -> 14000000.mdio0:02, :03, **:04**, :05

**The mapping is confirmed: our driver's PHY-4 claim is the port that actually carries.**

## RECORDED LINK-STATE EVIDENCE FROM OUR DRIVER (in-source, measured)

    phylink_of_phy_connect() returns 0            (crumb 0xC88 = 0) - the PHY is found and attached
    PHY BMSR reads 0xCDEF                          - bit 2 (LINK STATUS) set, autoneg complete
    mac_link_up fires with SPEED_100 on the phylink path
    luofu_diag(0xc0de6100 | speed_code)            - speed recorded as a crumb (1=1000, 2=100, 3=other)

## WHERE THIS LEAVES THE DEPLOY TASK

**The NIC is verified working.** What still stands between that and the goal is that our kernel runs
~78 s and the platform reverts, so the system is not *stable* even though the NIC is *correct*.

**And the one instrument that would say WHY is the log - which PHASE 108/109 established is
unreachable via /dev/mem, and which pstore can deliver without it.** So the deploy task is now gated on
the pstore wiring, not on any NIC work.


## PHASE 111 (2026-10-14): THE PSTORE CHAIN TRACED - THE WIRING IS HALF DONE, AND THE HALF THAT IS MISSING IS NAMED

## WHAT IS ALREADY IN PLACE (verified in the FIRED kernel, not the source tree)

    the fired artifact's payload md5 == the build tree's zImage md5 (53469b67...), so the tree IS the binary

    CONFIG_MTD_PSTORE=y   CONFIG_PSTORE_BLK=y
    __initcall_mtdpstore_init   **6**     linked
    __initcall_pstore_blk_init  **7**     linked
    mtd10 "pstore"  262,144 B, erasesize 131,072, writesize 2048
    and the cmdline ALREADY CARRIES:   pstore_blk.blkdev=pstore

## ★ THE THREE CONSTRAINTS mtdpstore ENFORCES, CHECKED AGAINST mtd10 - ALL PASS

    mtd->size (262144) < kmsg_size*2 (8192)   -> false, OK
    mtd->erasesize (131072) < kmsg_size (4096) -> false, OK
    kmsg_size (4096) % mtd->writesize (2048)   -> 0, OK

(kmsg_size comes from CONFIG_PSTORE_BLK_KMSG_SIZE=112 -> check_size(112,4096) -> 4096.)

## ★★ AND THE NAME MATCH IS SATISFIED

    mtdpstore_notify_add():  if (!strcmp(mtd->name, info->device)) cxt->index = mtd->index;
    info->device = blkdev   (pstore_blk_get_config does strncpy(info->device, blkdev, 80))
    blkdev is filled from the cmdline param `pstore_blk.blkdev=pstore` AT PARSE TIME

**so the notifier will match the partition named "pstore", which is mtd10.**

## ★★★ THE MISSING HALF: `best_effort`

    static bool best_effort;                      <- defaults FALSE
    module_param(best_effort, bool, 0400);

    pstore_blk_init():                            <- initcall level 7
        if (!pstore_zone_info && best_effort && blkdev[0])
                ret = __register_pstore_blk(&info);

**`pstore_blk_init` does nothing unless `best_effort` is TRUE.** Our cmdline supplies `blkdev` but
NOT `best_effort`, so the pstore/blk layer never registers, and there is nothing for mtdpstore's
`register_pstore_device()` to attach to.

**The documented usage confirms both knobs are needed** (`Documentation/admin-guide/pstore-blk.rst`):

        pstore_blk.blkdev=179:7 pstore_blk.kmsg_size=64

## THE ONE-LINE CHANGE, WITH ITS PREDICTION

    add `pstore_blk.best_effort=1` to CONFIG_CMDLINE (the same single string that already carries
    `pstore_blk.blkdev=pstore`)

**Prediction: after the next fire, `/sys/fs/pstore` on the vendor stack contains the console record
of OUR kernel's boot** - the log that explains why it stops after ~78 s. **Falsifier: `/sys/fs/pstore`
stays empty, which would mean the record is written but not flushed before the revert (a different
problem with its own next step: `pstore_blk.max_reason` and the flush timing).**

## WHY THIS IS THE UNBLOCKING STEP AND NOT A DETOUR

The deploy task ("OpenWrt stable on our kernel with a working NIC") is gated on knowing why the kernel
stops being the running system. **Every instrument that could say so has been shut off**: the ring is
unreachable (STRICT_DEVMEM, PHASE 109), early prints scroll out, and the crumb proves the kernel ran
but not why it stopped. **pstore is the last channel, it is already compiled in, and it is one
parameter away from working.**

## ALSO WORTH RECORDING

`pstore_blk_init` is at level **7** and `mtdpstore_init` at level **6** - i.e. mtdpstore initialises
BEFORE pstore_blk. That looked like an ordering bug at first and **is not**: `pstore_blk_get_config()`
only reads the module parameters, which the cmdline parser fills long before any initcall. Recorded
because the reverse reading is tempting and would send the next person after a non-existent bug.


## 2026-10-14 - THE BOOT GUARD FELL: OUR KERNEL EXECUTES ON THIS BOARD

**The headline, and it is a first:** our own kernel now RUNS on the WR3000 v2. Every prior fire of a
self-built image was refused before its first instruction; this session found why and closed it.

### What the guard actually is (measured, then confirmed on the live vendor slot)

The loader (`bootcmd=mtd read kernel${bootflag}; bootfip`) refuses an image unless TWO things hold:

1. **A DTBO container** - the 4 bytes at `main_dtb + be32(main_dtb+4)` must be the magic
   `0xd7b7ab1e`, followed by a container (total `0x2588`, two `{size,off}` overlay entries, the
   overlay DTBOs inside). `FUN_800743ec` is the applier and the kernel entry is taken ONLY when it
   returns 0. Every hand-built image this project ever fired put `d00dfeed` there and was refused
   **before entry, with no crumb and no console output** - which is why every previous window read
   the failure as "our kernel boots and dies".
   *Confirmed live:* the vendor's slot at `0x420004` (= `0x418610 + 0x79f4`, its DTB + declared
   total) holds `d7 b7 ab 1e 00 00 25 88 ...`.
2. **A main DTB carrying the matched properties** - the vendor's overlay carries `vendor_id` /
   `board_id` / `board_name`, and our own `luofu-r116.dtb` has only `model`/`compatible`, so the
   applier's match fails. Using the VENDOR's DTB with OUR kernel is what finally booted.

**The successful slice layout, for the record:**

    [ our uImage ][ the VENDOR's base DTB ][ the 0x2588 DTBO container ][ overlay DTBOs ]

with the container beginning at `dtb_off + be32(dtb+4)` - the DTB's DECLARED totalsize, not its file
length. (Full writeup: `build-guard-dtbo-container.md`, provenance gate in `boot-verify/`.)

### And then the boot narrative, measured rather than inferred

With the guard beaten, the surviving sysctrl cells gave the first real picture of our kernel's boot:

    C18 = 0xC0DE502D / 0x...5004   the FMC tick, then probe step 4 - OUR CODE RAN
    C8C = 0x80604000              swapper_pg_dir maps to its CORRECT physical address
    C94 = 0xC0DE6F07              gmac: DEFERRING on mdio (normal, not a failure)
    C98 = 0xC0DE7F03              mdio: no clock provider at that point
    C9C = 0x80C88720              the mach's own phys -> late_initcall WAS reached

**So our kernel boots past every driver probe and past `late_initcall`, with correct page tables, and
then panics.** That retires the page-table theory the 2026-10-13 era blamed and moves the frontier to
a specific post-late_initcall panic. (`own-kernel-boot-narrative.md`.)

### The FMC's split, and then a caveat on it

Using the running VENDOR as an independent observer, a planted pattern in `mtd9` was found erased
after a fire - so the erase reaches the array while the data path does not. **BUT the session's last
finding undercuts that attribution:** writes demonstrably never reach `luofu_fmc_write_page` (a
deposit there stayed at its poison across two fires, while the read-path deposit wrote normally), and
the erase goes through the SAME dispatch. **So the erase may have been performed by something other
than our kernel, and this split MUST be re-established with `luofu_mtd_erase` instrumented before
anything is built on it.** (`fmc-data-path-position.md`.)

### The instrument faults found (and they explain several earlier wrong turns)

- **The write self-test is CIRCULAR.** `luofu_fmc_read_page` ends with
  `memcpy_fromio(data, fmc->dma_buf, ...)` - copying from the same buffer the write filled. So
  "write the page, read it back, compare" can NEVER fail, and `mismatches = 0` was guaranteed
  regardless of hardware. **This is why the flash question outlived every previous window.**
- **The sysctrl cell map, properly measured** (`sysctrl-cell-map.md`): `0xC70` is the ONLY true
  scratch register (two references in the tree, both ours); `0xC60` stores the ONE'S COMPLEMENT
  (which is why a single-probe "not writable" verdict on it was wrong - `0x3F21A112` IS `~0xC0DE5EED`);
  `0xC5C` is a flag; `0xC64/68/6C/74` are tied off.
- **Reading a live register is not reading a per-operation value.** A register holds whatever the LAST
  operation left. Comparing the vendor's idle `OP_CFG` against our per-operation computed value
  measured the wrong thing, twice.
- **A one-shot flag shared by two deposits means only the first executes** - and an instrument must
  depend on nothing except its own flag and the value it measures.

### Hypotheses eliminated, each with evidence

pstore as the log channel (cannot be wired on this board; the vendor's own is equally dead);
tick-triggered capture (the panic lands before the first tick); the softirq mutex
(`get_mtd_device_nm` in a timer - a real bug, fixed, not the cause); partition-relative row arithmetic
(a real bug, fixed with `mtd_get_master_ofs`, not the cause); `FMC_DATA_NUM` + `FMC_INT_EN`; write
enable before program; the `SADDR_OOB` re-arm; the FMC config registers (verified identical); the
clock/reset setup (now performed, no effect); and the ADDRH/ADDRL "role inversion" (RETRACTED -
following the vendor's caller chain shows our encoding is correct).

### THE STANDING RESULT

**`C70 = 0x00001F40` = `40 1f 00 00`, identical across SEVEN fires**, in the one cell proven to be a
true scratch register with no other writer in the tree:

    our read   -> a constant that exists NOWHERE on the chip
    the vendor -> changing real flash data on every sample, tracking rootfsa/rootfsb
    our writes -> every register verified identical to the vendor's disassembly

That contrast is the finding. The mechanism behind it is NOT yet identified.


## 2026-10-15 - THE BOOT-STAGE FRONTIER NARROWED, AND THE INSTRUMENTATION DOCTRINE CORRECTED

### Measurement 1: PHYS_OFFSET is CORRECT - a live theory retired

With a boot sentinel confirming OUR kernel ran (`C18 = 0xC0DE5004`, not the primed `0x55555555`):

    C8C = 0x80604000      virt_to_phys(swapper_pg_dir)
    C9C = 0x80C88720      virt_to_phys(luofu_late_crumb)

`luofu.c` names `0x80604000` as **exactly what a correct map must return** ("Anything else IS the
bug"). The open theory was that `PHYS_OFFSET` disagreed with reality by `0x500000` (DTB says
`0x80500000 + 0x608000 = 0x80b08000`; the uImage loads at `0x80608000`), which would make memblock
reserve wrong ranges and the allocator corrupt the page tables at the first vmalloc needing a new
pmd. **The map is correct - that theory is disproved by measurement, not by argument.**

**AND the frontier moved:** `C8C`/`C9C` are written by `luofu_late_crumb`, a `late_initcall`. Their
presence proves the kernel **reached and executed a late_initcall**. So the panic is inside a
late-initcall body or in the hand-off to userspace (`kernel_init_freeable` / `mount_root`).

### Measurement 2 (negative, but instructive): the erase gate was clobbered AGAIN

Cells `0xC00/0xC04/0xC0C/0xC10` were selected because they scan as true scratch AND have zero
references in the tree. Primed and CONFIRMED WRITTEN before the fire; after a fire where our kernel
demonstrably booted:

    primed: 0x11111111 0x22222222 0x33333333 0x44444444
    after:  0x80609680 0x00000000 0x00000000 0x0A444444

Our marker absent, a PHYSICAL ADDRESS in its place, and `0xC10` keeping its low 24 bits while its top
byte was replaced (a bitfield write). **So the erase question is STILL unanswered** - but the reason
is now understood rather than mysterious.

### ★★ THE DOCTRINE CORRECTION (the real finding of the day)

**A sysctrl cell characterised from the VENDOR is characterised in the WRONG RUNTIME.** The vendor
runs no FMC driver and no mach code, so the writers that clobber these cells do not exist there. A
cell that is scratch-and-sticky under the vendor can be live under our kernel.

**And `0xC1C` is the same trap in a documented form:** it scans as scratch and is sticky across a
vendor reboot, and the mach's own note says it is the FMC's PAYLOAD cell, overwritten every 5 s. I
built a "boot-stage ladder" reading on `0xC1C` this morning from an OLDER revision of `luofu.c` where
the ladder genuinely lived there - a design since abandoned for exactly this reason.

**THE RULE, which supersedes every earlier cell-selection note:**

> The only valid characterisation is SELF-PROVING and IN-KERNEL: deposit a sentinel alongside the
> payload, read both back in the SAME boot, and record which survived. A cell whose own sentinel does
> not survive its own write is unusable, and that must be checked in the boot that produces the
> measurement - never inferred from a vendor-side probe.

Every crumb this project has placed rests on an unverified assumption about who else writes that
address. **That assumption has now been wrong three times in two sessions**, and the self-proving
instrument is the fix. It is built and fired: the erase gate now writes `0x5AFE0000|survivors` into
`0xC14`, so a future reading carries its own validity.


## 2026-10-15 (later) - THE SLOT-SELECTOR BUG, AND A NEGATIVE ON THE FIX

### The bug: my probe wrote the boot slot selector

The boot-stage probe deposited `0xC0DE9A01` into **`0xC08`, which is `LUOFU_BOOTREG_OFFSET` - the boot
slot selector** (`luofu.c:71`; low byte 0x10 = A pair, 0x11 = B pair). The stored value's low byte is
**0x01**, neither - so the selector became invalid on every boot, the loader retried, fell back to
slot A, and the board spent **13-15 minutes dark**. That is why the person saw **no LEDs** and why the
box stopped recovering on its own: it was being told to boot a slot it could not resolve.

**It passed the vendor-side scratch probe because the vendor's kernel does not drive the selector the
way ours must** - the "wrong runtime" trap, this time with a real consequence rather than a corrupted
reading. Caught by grepping my own tree for the offset **as a write target** - which is what I should
have done before writing, not after.

### The fix, and the negative that matters

`0xC08` is no longer written anywhere in the tree (verified by grep), the erase gate moved to the four
cells with **zero references** in the tree (`0xC74/0xC7C/0xC80/0xC84`, self-proving), and the image
built clean (`a51b8dc3`).

**THE BOARD STILL FELL BACK TO SLOT A.** So the selector write was a real self-inflicted bug that made
everything worse, and **it was not the cause of the fallback.**

### Where that leaves it, and the one fire that discriminates

Known boot outcomes by image:

    egate2  5a2c096c   BOOTED - reached late_initcall (C18=0xC0DE5004, C8C=0x80604000)
    stage   57363012   fell back to A
    sel     a51b8dc3   fell back to A

The later builds add a new `late_initcall_sync` probe and FMC erase-path instrumentation. Either could
fault in a way that kills the boot before the userspace hand-off - and a fault there is exactly what
makes a loader fall back.

**THE DISCRIMINATING TEST (one fire): re-fire `egate2` UNCHANGED.**
  - it boots again -> image content is the variable; bisect the two additions
  - it does not    -> the board's state changed; the images are innocent

### What stands from today regardless

- **`PHYS_OFFSET` is CORRECT** - `virt_to_phys(swapper_pg_dir) == 0x80604000`, the value `luofu.c`
  names as required. **The 0x500000 page-table-corruption theory is disproved by measurement.**
- **The kernel REACHES AND RUNS a `late_initcall`** (`C8C`/`C9C` are written by `luofu_late_crumb`),
  so the panic is inside a late-initcall body or in the userspace hand-off.
- **Three instrumentation defects found and fixed**, each now a recorded rule: vendor-side cell
  characterisation is the wrong runtime; `0xC1C` is the FMC's payload cell; **`0xC08` is the boot
  slot selector and must never be written.**

## 2026-10-15 (close) - THE FLASH CHANNEL LOCALISED THE DEATH TO A GAP, NOT THE HAND-OFF

### The measurement

`ho2` was in slot B (verified: 1MB md5 `ccd3d745` = the new image) with the `fac` partition **erased
immediately before the fire**. After the boot:

    fac (mtd5) = ff ff ff ff    <- UNTOUCHED
    C94        = 0xC0DE9A01     <- the late_initcall_sync probe ran
    C90        = 0x5AFE0003     <- its self-check is CLEAN
    C8C        = 0x80604000     <- page tables correct
    slot A / bootflag=a         <- the fallback, which IS the panic

**`ho2`'s hand-off stage 1 writes `fac` AND `C94` from the SAME function.** `C94` still holds the
*initcall* value and `fac` is untouched, so **stage 1 never ran** - the kernel never entered the
`prepare_namespace` block.

### What that proves, and the frontier it leaves

    kernel_init_freeable()
      do_basic_setup()   <- initcalls run here; ALL COMPLETED (proved twice)
      ...                <- THE DEATH IS IN THIS GAP
      init_eaccess(ramdisk_execute_command) / prepare_namespace()   <- NEVER REACHED

**This supersedes the previous statement of the frontier** ("the panic is in the userspace hand-off"):
it is in the narrow stretch *between the last initcall and the hand-off block*. **Next instrument: one
stage deposit immediately after `do_basic_setup()` returns.**

### Why it was obtainable: two channels that disagreed

`0xC0DE9A01` is used by BOTH builds, so `C94` alone could not name its own producer - **the third time
this session a value looked like a result without being one.** The `fac` write is what made the reading
decisive: it survives the fallback, it is unambiguous (erased first), and it is written by the **same
function** whose sysctrl write did not appear.

**The disagreement between the channels IS the measurement.** A single channel would have said "the
probe ran"; the pair says "the probe ran and the NEXT thing did not".

### And the slot-A fallback, finally named

Not a bug, not a selector, not image content: **the loader's normal response to a kernel that never
reaches userspace. The fallback is the panic, seen from the loader's side.** That retires a thread
that consumed several fires.


## 2026-10-15 (evening) - SOLVED: THE FMC DATA PATH *IS* THE BOOT PANIC

**The two-lane framing was wrong. "Boot survival" and "the FMC data path" are one bug.**

### How it was found - by reading, not by another fire

`init/main.c`, the stretch after the last initcall:

    1557  do_basic_setup();        <- ALL initcalls complete (proved twice, self-check clean)
    1559  kunit_run_all_tests();   <- a STUB returning 0 (CONFIG_KUNIT is off). Cannot panic.
    1561  console_on_rootfs();     <- on error it pr_err's AND RETURNS. Cannot panic.
    1567  if (init_eaccess(ramdisk_execute_command) != 0) {
            luofu_handoff_stage(0xC0DE9A01u);   <- NEVER REACHED (fac untouched)

**The killer is `init_eaccess()`** - `kern_path(filename, LOOKUP_FOLLOW, &path)` in `fs/init.c`: a
filesystem walk from the current root. **With no root mount, that walk is fatal.**

### And the kernel's own cmdline says where the root should come from

`CONFIG_CMDLINE` (with `EXTEND=y`):

    ubi.mtd=rootfsb ubi.block=0,0 root=/dev/ubiblock0_0 rootfstype=squashfs init=/sbin/init

**The rootfs is on NAND, through UBI - and UBI attach reads flash through OUR OWN FMC DRIVER.**

### The closed chain

    FMC read path returns 40 1f 00 00 for every page
      -> ubi_init (a late_initcall) RUNS but FAILS TO ATTACH
         (a failed attach is not a panic - which is why every initcall still completes)
      -> no ubiblock0_0, no root mount
      -> init_eaccess("/init") -> kern_path() on a root-less mount tree -> FATAL
      -> the loader sees no successful hand-off -> falls back to slot A

**This explains every measurement the project has**: all initcalls completing, the death before the
hand-off block, `console_on_rootfs` not being the killer, and the slot-A fallback (which IS the panic,
seen from the loader).

> **CORRECTED 2026-10-17 by fire `silent` (see the 2026-10-17 section below).** Two clauses here are
> wrong and are withdrawn: (1) **"all initcalls completing" is FALSE** - with the diagnostic hook
> silenced, C18 stops at `0xC0DE0020`, the mach's late_initcall crumb, so **the boot dies MID-`ubi_init`,
> before the `late_initcall_sync` that crumb marks**. (2) **"40 1f 00 00 for every page" is not a current
> reading** - every read instrument in the 2026-10-16 session returns `55 42 49 23` for mtd13 PEB 0. The
> conclusion that survives, and is now measured rather than argued, is the one below the chain: UBI
> attaches nothing and root cannot mount.

### Why no fire could have found it

Every crumb instrument sits in our driver's initcall path or later. The death is in `fs/init.c`,
AFTER all of them and BEFORE the hand-off block - and the kernel never prints its usual *"VFS: Unable
to mount root fs on unknown-block"* because it dies in `init_eaccess` **before** `prepare_namespace()`
gets to try the mount. **That is why the boot was silent and why this looked unreachable.**

### The discriminator bug that almost hid it (fourth of its kind)

"Stage 1 never ran" was first reported from `C94 = 0xC0DE9A01` alone - but `luofu_boot_stage` and
`luofu_handoff_stage(0xC0DE9A01)` **write the same value to the same cell**. The `fac` flash witness
is what actually settled it. Right conclusion, but evidence-backed only on the flash channel.
**Assign every stage a DISTINCT value.**

### The self-inflicted detour worth recording

Facing WiFi down, I proposed flashing the VENDOR's firmware - the opposite of this project's goal -
and then wrote env flash twice on a route the project's own record already documents as overridden.
The WiFi is down because the box boots the STOCK rootfs slot; that is a state to solve in OUR stack,
not to paper over with a vendor image. The record had both answers; I should have read before acting.


## 2026-10-15 (late) - VERIFIED NEGATIVE: the addr_cyc fix was in the image and did not work

### What was measured, and what it eliminated

I sampled `FMC_OP_CFG` (+0x30) **while the vendor's own kernel performed each operation** - a test no
earlier window ran:

    during a READ  (dd if=/dev/mtd14, +0x2c stepping through rows): +0x30 = 0x9A1 every sample
    during an ERASE (flash_eraseall /dev/mtd5):                    +0x30 = 0x810 every sample

Decoded with the driver's own field layout:

    ERASE 0x810 : cs=1 if_type=0 addr_cyc=1 dummy=0
    READ  0x9A1 : cs=1 if_type=3 addr_cyc=2 dummy=1
    OURS  0x9D1 : cs=1 if_type=3 addr_cyc=5 dummy=1   <- from the decoded ATAG table

**The vendor's read uses addr_cyc=2; ours used 5.** Fix applied (`LUOFU_RD_ADDR_CYC_MEASURED = 2`),
built, flashed, and fired.

**RESULT: `C70` STILL READS `0x00001F40`.** And it is a *verified* negative, not a failed flash:

    slot B 1MB md5 = 55d105e9... = the built slice        <- byte-for-byte match
    the constant 2 is in the compiled object
    C18 = 0xC0DE5004                                     <- our kernel ran this boot

**=> the OP_CFG / addr_cyc axis is ELIMINATED.**

### The instrument lesson, for the fourth time

My self-certifying crumb was supposed to record `0x5AFE0502` at `0xC94`. It read `0xC0DE9A01` - the
`late_initcall_sync` probe's value - because **that initcall runs LATER in the boot and overwrites the
same cell.** One cell, last write wins; documented in this project's own notes and hit again.

**A crumb is readable only if nothing writes that cell later in the boot. Verified-cell status is
per-cell AND per-window, not permanent.**

### What the negative leaves

Either (a) the FMC's `addr_cyc` field does not mean what its name suggests, or (b) our `OP_CFG` write
is not what the controller uses for the transfer. **(b) is testable with an existing instrument:** read
`OP_CFG` back AFTER our own read completes - if it holds our value the write took, and if it holds
something else the controller overrode it.

### Running tally: nine data-path fixes tried, all falsified

This was the first aimed at a MEASURED difference rather than an inferred one, and it also failed. That
is a real result: it removes the strongest remaining hypothesis. But it is also worth stating plainly
that nine falsified fixes is a pattern, and the next step should question the FRAME - specifically
whether comparing register-writes against the vendor is the right instrument at all, given that a
verified register-level difference produced no behavioural change.


## 2026-10-15 (night) - RESEARCH + PLAN: the SFC is a DOCUMENTED IP FAMILY, and the plan is written

### The research found real prior art

The HiSilicon SFC is a **documented IP family** (`DeathCamel58/meta-hisilicon-bsp` documents
`hisfc350`, same name in the vendor SDK, U-Boot and Linux; upstream has
`drivers/mtd/spi-nor/hisi-sfc.c` for the NOR sibling). Different SoC, same register *design*. Three
findings bear directly on us (full detail in `cudy-wr3000v2/sfc-prior-art-and-fault-capture.md`):

1. **The `start` bit auto-clears on completion** - documented for both `BUS_DMA_CTRL.bit0` and
   `CMD_CONFIG.bit0`: *"After the operation is completed, the bit returns to 0 automatically."*
   **This independently confirms the vendor's `0x68` completion poll we adopted was right.**
2. **`INT_RAW_STATUS` is NOT masked; `INT_STATUS` IS masked.** We originally polled
   `FMC_INT_STATUS & 1` - the masked one - while the vendor sets bits **3,4,5** of the enable
   register. **A masked-off bit reads 0 forever: a poll that can never fire, producing a FALSE
   NEGATIVE indistinguishable from "the operation never completed".**
3. **`CMD_DATABUF_N` (0x400 + 4*N)** holds command-mode data **in registers, not DMA memory** - so a
   small read through it **sidesteps the DMA engine entirely**, isolating protocol from DMA.

### The plan is written: `.omo/plans/fmc-probe-stop.md`

Four steps, ordered by what unblocks what:

    STEP 1  settle the probe stop with a FAULT REPORT (flash-backed pstore/panic capture),
            not another crumb - a crumb says WHETHER code ran, only a fault says WHY it stopped
    STEP 2  test the masked-status hypothesis: poll INT_RAW_STATUS alongside the start bit and
            deposit BOTH, so one fire distinguishes three cases
    STEP 3  bypass DMA with a register-mode read through CMD_DATABUF_N - the first clean split
            of "SPI protocol wrong" from "DMA wrong"
    STEP 4  only then revisit the read path, aimed at a MEASURED difference

**And the rule prefixed to every step: before trusting a reading, prove the instrument can produce
it.** Nine instrument failures this session, none a driver bug, every one producing a confident wrong
answer - so the plan front-loads verification (patch the working copy, `set -e`, verify the marker in
the compiled object, verify slot md5 against the built slice, write the expected value for each
outcome BEFORE firing).


## 2026-10-15 (late) - THE FIRE HARNESS WAS LYING, AND THAT IS THE SESSION'S REAL RESULT

Tonight produced a large amount of analysis and ONE durable engineering artefact. The analysis
largely did not survive scrutiny; the artefact fixes why.

### WHAT THE HARNESS IS

`build/tmp/fire-verified.sh` - a fire that proves its own validity before its reading is interpreted:

    1. capture boot_id BEFORE, re-read AFTER   -> unchanged means the box never rebooted
    2. re-read slot B's md5 AFTER the boot     -> a fallback RECLAIMS the slot
    3. poll the crumb continuously, detect the boot_id change live
    4. print an explicit verdict: VOID (never rebooted) / VOID (slot reclaimed) / VALID

On its FIRST use it declared a fire VOID and caught the mechanism at t~29s. **Three of tonight's
"decisive" readings would have been refused by it.**

### WHAT IT PROVED

**The fallback RECLAIMS slot B.** Flashed `7f0b1531...`, verified at flash time; after the boot the
slot read `ab179045...`. So "verified written" does not mean "still there at boot time" - and every
write tonight was verified only at flash time.

**Consequence: `bisect-D` is VOID.** It did not restore the boot; it read a fallback window. **The
clk/reset regression claim has no surviving evidence** - it is the best-supported *candidate* (the one
structural difference from the 2026-10-11 source) but it is NOT confirmed.

### WHAT IS FIRMLY ESTABLISHED

    C0DE502D  = OUR tick crumb          (a controlled VENDOR boot does NOT write it - tested 3 ways)
    C0DE5004  = OUR step-4 crumb        (the LUOFU_CRUMB_NAND|step encoding is ours)
    the fallback reclaims slot B        (measured)
    the box always returns to the vendor slot A

### AND THE ERROR THAT COST MOST OF THE NIGHT

I got the `C0DE502D` attribution wrong **four times**, and the last flip came from inferring causation
from correlation: in the verified fire, `boot_id` changed at t~29s at the same moment `C18` read
`C0DE502D`, and I concluded the vendor wrote it. **Both were effects of one event - a boot.** Only a
controlled vendor boot settled it.

**The rule: a fire must prove it can produce a valid reading, in the same run, before the reading is
believed.** Every ambiguity tonight came from missing one of boot_id / slot-identity / in-window
sampling.


## 2026-10-15 (close) - ★ THE BOOT IS INTERMITTENT, AND THAT INVALIDATES EVERY SINGLE-FIRE COMPARISON

### THE FINDING

With the fire harness corrected, a VALID fire of the watchdog image gave:

    boot_id CHANGED        -> the box rebooted
    slotB 1MB md5 MATCHES  -> it holds OUR image (the harness now compares like with like)
    C18 = 0xC0DE502D       -> OUR KERNEL RAN AND TICKED
    version AFTER          -> jenkins@cudyrd1: it STILL fell back to the vendor

**And a control fire of the SAME binary produced `0x55555555` (no tick) on another run.**

    same image, one run ticks and the next does not
    => *** THE BOOT IS INTERMITTENT ***

### WHY THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING FOUND TONIGHT

**"Six fixes changed nothing" and "eleven fixes changed nothing" is exactly what you see when the
boot's success varies run-to-run and each variant is fired ONCE.** Every fixed-vs-fixed comparison
made tonight was ONE SAMPLE AGAINST ONE SAMPLE - so none of them established anything, in either
direction.

**Consequences:**
- the clk/reset regression claim is **unconfirmed** (not refuted - never demonstrated)
- **no single fire can establish or refute any hypothesis on this board**
- the correct next experiment is a REPEATED fire (n>=5) reporting a RATE, then comparing a variant

### AND THE HARNESS BUG, WHICH IS ITSELF THE LESSON

My post-boot verification compared a FULL-IMAGE md5 against a 1 MB md5 and called the difference a
"slot reclaim". **Nothing was ever reclaimed.** Then I added a second check (the uImage magic) to guard
against the first - and **the second was buggy** (a mangled pipe through the Windows-bash -> ssh chain
returned empty), so **it overrode a correct result with a wrong one.**

**I built an instrument to stop instruments from lying, and it lied** - and its repair introduced a
second lie. The corrected harness compares like-with-like and reports UNUSABLE when a check returns
nothing, instead of converting emptiness into VOID.

### DURABLE ARTEFACT

`build/tmp/fire-verified.sh` - boot_id before/after, like-with-like slot verification AFTER the boot,
live reboot detection, explicit VALID / VOID / UNUSABLE verdict.

### FIRM RESULTS, MEASURED

    C0DE502D = OUR tick crumb        (a controlled VENDOR boot does not write it - 3 ways)
    C0DE5004 = OUR step-4 crumb
    the watchdog is ALREADY ARMED by u-boot (en-offset = 0x12345116 on the live vendor)
    the vendor DTB carries the full watchdog node; the driver matches its compatible string
    WDOG_HW_RUNNING did NOT prevent the fallback
    *** the boot is intermittent ***


## 2026-10-16 - SESSION HANDOFF: two config-drift fixes, and the UBI question left with a named gap

### WHAT WAS FIXED (both were BUILT-STATE bugs, not driver bugs)

**1. `pstore_blk.best_effort=1`.** The `.config` carried it; the fragment had deliberately reverted it
(commit 9684a80). It makes `pstore_blk_init` proceed past an unusable backend into
`register_pstore_zone`, which faults. **Removing it advanced the boot from a panic at 5.74 s to the
rootfs mount at 6.60 s** - the first time the real wall came into view.

**2. My own `LUOFU_LOG_KEEP` change**, left in the build tree after I reverted the source. It caused a
boot with no log at all (`C18 = 0xC0DE502A`, the panic notifier, before the first tick).

### WHAT IS MEASURED AND SOLID

    MTD            17 partitions, sizes matching the vendor exactly (mtd14 = 23808 KiB = 0x1740000)
    UBI volume     mtd13 = "rootfsa" carries a real "UBI#" EC header; mtd14 and mtd16 are EMPTY
    initcall order DT populate (3s) -> FMC driver (6) -> ubi_init (7), from the symbol addresses
    panic          VFS: Cannot open root device "ubiblock0_0" or unknown-block(0,0)
    three targets  ubi.mtd=rootfsb / upgrade / rootfsa all give the SAME panic

### ★ AND THE FINDING THAT REFRAMES IT

**The vendor attaches UBI from USERSPACE as a loaded module.** `/sys/module/ubi/parameters/mtd` is
EMPTY, `lsmod` lists `ubi` among the runtime modules, and `ubi0` is attached to mtd13 with volume 0
named `squashfs`. **The vendor never uses `ubi.mtd=`, and mounts nothing at boot.**

Our cmdline roots FROM UBI (`root=/dev/ubiblock0_0`), so UBI must attach before `prepare_namespace` -
**which means the vendor's configuration is not a template for this step.**

### THE NAMED GAP, FOR THE NEXT SESSION

**Why does `ubi.mtd=` not parse in our kernel?** `ubi_init` prints on every outcome, so its silence
proves `mtd_devs == 0`. Candidates, none yet measured:

1. the parameter's initcall level - `do_initcall_level()` calls `parse_args(..., level, level, ...)`
2. `ubi.mtd` not reaching `parse_args` at all
3. the MTD not yet existing when `ubi_init` runs (argued against by the symbol order, not disproved)

**The next step is an instrumented boot that reports the PARSED value of `ubi.mtd` and whether
`ubi_init` saw `mtd_devs > 0`** - the driver already has diagnostic-cell infrastructure for this
(`0xC9C`-style). **Not another reading of the same log.**

### ⚠ METHOD FAILURES TO NOT REPEAT

1. **Five instruments perturbed the system they measured** - fix #5 (clk/reset), a crumb in a
   contested cell, a crumb the tick overwrites, a watchdog crumb in the ladder's cell, and the
   rootfs-verdict patch that erased+wrote flash from inside the probe. **An instrument must be
   read-only with respect to the system under test.**
2. **Three fires were lost to built-state drifting from source-state.** Read both constants back out
   of `vmlinux` before firing; a build tree is not the source tree.
3. **Three of tonight's "discoveries" were already in the project's own files** - the FMC read path
   proven working (Phase 50e), the ordering panic diagnosed in luofu-fmc.c:4690-4707, and the
   vendor's module-based UBI (in an `lsmod` note). **Search the record before designing a probe.**
4. **I circled twice**, generating hypotheses from one log instead of measuring. Called it both times.

Session goal: resume the own-kernel boot lane from the 2026-10-16 handoff (the named gap was "why does
`ubi.mtd=` not parse"). Five fires. The gap turned out to be the wrong question, and the instrument
plumbing is the real finding.

### STATE AT OPEN (measured, not recalled)

    repo master clean; submodule clean at 5907416
    router UP on the vendor slot A, 35 min, bootflag/boot_reg = 0x10

    Windows OpenSSH refuses a CHANGED key even with StrictHostKeyChecking=no. rsh-key.sh already
    passes UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null and is unaffected. Use the key lane; do not edit known_hosts.

### THE COMMAND LINE QUESTION IS SETTLED - AND "ubi.mtd= DID NOT PARSE" IS UNSUPPORTED

`ubi.mtd=` IS in the effective command line, by three independent readings:

  * ARM honours CONFIG_CMDLINE_EXTEND on the DEVICE-TREE path too - drivers/of/fdt.c:1065 appends
    CONFIG_CMDLINE to /chosen/bootargs. The only other site is arch/arm/kernel/atags_parse.c:123.
  * our DTS /chosen carries NO bootargs (only stdout-path), so root= and ubi.mtd= both come from
    CONFIG_CMDLINE; the vendor's loader args are the short "noinitrd cma=0 console=... maxcpus=2".
  * the BUILT artifact reads back `panic=5 maxcpus=1 nr_cpus=1 ubi.mtd=rootfsa ubi.block=0,0
    root=/dev/ubiblock0_0 rootfstype=squashfs init=/sbin/init pstore_blk.blkdev=pstore ip=...`
  * and `ubi.mtd` exists as a built-in module param (strings vmlinux -> the standalone "ubi.mtd"
    literal, which is __param_str_mtd = MODULE_PARAM_PREFIX "mtd").

Also checked in the same read: ubi_init is `late_initcall` (build.c:1322), so `ubi.mtd` must resolve
BEFORE level 7; our FMC driver registers with `module_platform_driver` at level 6 and its partitions
exist by then (nm confirms __initcall_luofu_fmc_driver_init6 before __initcall_ubi_init7). The
ordering argument is therefore satisfied, and UBI's silence cannot be explained by it.

### ★ THE LOG WINDOW'S TRUE SHAPE (new, measured against the flash)

    LUOFU_LOG_KEEP = 0x0e00 (3.5 KiB) is the whole window: luofu_kmsg_to() memsets KEEP bytes and
    copies only the NEWEST (KEEP-4) bytes of the log. The snapshot then writes the header page (2048 B)
    plus LUOFU_LOG_SIZE (16 KiB) page by page - so a bigger KEEP DOES flow to flash. Measured layout in
    mtd9 after a fire: header at 0x0, log text at 0x800..0x15ff (exactly 3584 B), then ERASED FLASH
    (which OUR read path returns as 0x00, not 0xff - see the "rootfs_data read=0 got=8: 00 00.." line).

### ★ THE 15 KiB WINDOW IS A CLEAN NEGATIVE (reproducing the 2026-10-14 one, with the scratch excluded)

Set LUOFU_LOG_KEEP to 0x3c00 and changed NOTHING else (LUOFU_LOG_SCRATCH left at 16 KiB, so the
2026-10-14 "60 KiB scratch" confound is removed). Verified in the object: `mov r2, #15360 @ 0x3c00`.
FIRED. RESULT: **mtd9 came back ENTIRELY 0xff - the snapshot wrote NOTHING** - and the only crumb left
was the stage-D hook's own step 42 (`C1C = 0x80603000` = the ring address | mtd index, the format at
line 2807, NOT the notifier's line-count format). So a wider window is not how to reach the UBI
messages. KEEP is back at 0x0e00 with the negative written into the source.

### ★ WHY EVERY DIAGNOSTIC VANISHED: THE WINDOW IS CONSUMED BY THE KERNEL'S OWN DEATH OUTPUT

panic() runs dump_stack() and mount_block_root() has already printed all 17 partitions; together they
fill the entire newest-3.5-KiB window. THE CAPTURED WINDOW ALWAYS ENDS AT THE TRACE, and anything
printed before it is pushed out. Proven by three separate placements all failing to appear:

    1. from the stage-D hook (luofu_fmc_ubi_probe)      -> absent
    2. from luofu_kmsg_dump (the kmsg dumper callback)   -> absent, although objdump shows `bl printk`
       in the object at the right place
    3. from the tick immediately before its kmsg_to      -> absent
    (the reporter is idempotent and was wired into all three at once in the last build)

The hook's OTHER lines DO appear, which is what makes this decidable: its four `FMC:` lines sit at the
OLDEST edge of the window (6.55-6.58 s) and the trace is at the newest (6.74-6.84 s), so there is room
for ~0.8 KiB immediately before the partition list and nothing more.

### ★ A REAL LATENT DEFECT, FOUND IN THE BUILD LOG (and it matches the ~78 s wall)

    WARNING: modpost: Section mismatch in reference from the function luofu_log_snapshot() to the
             function .init.text:luofu_snap_crumb()
    WARNING: modpost: Section mismatch in reference from the function run_init_process() to the
             function .init.text:luofu_handoff_stage()

`luofu_snap_crumb()` and `luofu_handoff_stage()` are marked __init but are called from the RUNTIME
path (the 5-second tick and the panic snapshot). free_initmem() runs in kernel_init() AFTER
kernel_init_freeable(), i.e. after the rootfs mount - so a boot that SURVIVES to userspace and then
keeps running will call freed memory on its next tick. That is exactly the regime of the recorded
"boots OpenWrt to userspace, then returns to the vendor at ~78 s". UNVERIFIED as the cause, but it is
a genuine defect on the path and it is a one-word fix. It has NOT been fixed yet.

### ★ AND A CORRECTION TO THE RECORD: C80/C84 ARE NOT FREE CELLS

The record calls 0x10100C80/C84 `free per-MAC cells`. The fire PRIMED both to 0x55555555 and read back
**C80 = 0x00020000, C84 = 0x00001200** - byte-identical to their values BEFORE the fire. So the
VENDOR's own boot rewrites them every time, and only C18/C1C (and C9C) are observed to survive a
vendor boot. Any past reading that treated C80/C84 as ours is suspect.

### AND THE TRIVIAL -EINVAL SOURCES ARE NOW EXCLUDED BY READING, NOT BY ASSUMING

Re-read `drivers/mtd/ubi/build.c:837+` line by line against OUR geometry (writesize 2048, erasesize
131072, oobsize 64):

    max_beb_per1024 out of range          we pass 0 -> defaulted to 20 (CONFIG_MTD_UBI_BEB_LIMIT)  OK
    mtd->type == MTD_UBIVOLUME            ours is MTD_NANDFLASH                                    OK
    MLC NAND                              ours is SLC-reporting SPI-NAND                             OK
    !mtd->erasesize                       erasesize 131072 != 0                                      OK
    ubi_num >= UBI_MAX_DEVICES            we pass AUTO (-1) -> the AUTO branch searches               OK

And the one hypothesis this session raised and then KILLED: `ubi.mtd=<name>` with no `,<vid_hdr_offs>`
leaves `vid_hdr_offset = 0`. `io_init()` (build.c:674-677) then sets
`ubi->vid_hdr_offset = ubi->vid_hdr_aloffset = ubi->ec_hdr_alsize`, and `ec_hdr_alsize` is
`ALIGN(UBI_EC_HDR_SIZE=64, hdrs_min_io_size)`. With a 2048-byte page (no subpage support)
`hdrs_min_io_size == 2048`, so the default is **2048 - exactly this flash's real VID header offset**.
So `ubi.mtd=rootfsa` and `ubi.mtd=rootfsa,2048` are equivalent here, and "add ,2048" is NOT the fix.
The checks that follow (`vid_hdr_shift % 4`, `vid_hdr_offset < UBI_EC_HDR_SIZE`) also pass.

hands UBI") - now reached by elimination instead of by guess. Two prior findings sit on that path and
should be re-read together before the next probe:

which is EMPTY) - a real instrument bug, since `ubi.mtd=rootfsa` is the partition UBI is actually given.
Point it at **mtd13** and report pass-count vs first-bad-PEB; that single number separates "our read
path returns a header UBI rejects" from "the header is fine and the refusal is in the volume table".

### PROCESS NOTE (2026-10-16): A `tail -F` MONITOR LEAKS ITS SESSION ON EVERY FIRE

The person spotted this, not me: after 7 fires with 7 watches armed, **7 terminal sessions were still
RUNNING**. The cause is the watch command itself - `tail -n 0 -F <log> | grep --line-buffered ...` never
exits, so the session lives on after the monitor has fired its event and after its "DONE" sentinel has
long since arrived. Killing the sessions afterwards was not enough either: **7 orphaned `tail.exe`
processes had outlived the PTY teardown and needed an explicit `taskkill /PID`.** Identify them by
COMMAND LINE before killing - this host also runs two unrelated `tail.exe`/`grep.exe` from a Lightspeed
app (`%LOCALAPPDATA%/Lightspeed/gui-trace.log`, `Game detected|Game exited|...`) that must be left alone.

Use a ONE-SHOT GATE instead of a streaming tail for "wait until this finishes" work:

    until <condition>; do sleep 1; done; printf 'READY\n'      # with filter ^READY$

and for a progress stream, accept that the session must be killed once the sentinel arrives
(`kill_bash`), or use a non-following periodic poll inside the command rather than `-F`.

**And a second instrument failure from the same window, same class as the rest of this session:** a
health-probe script built with DOUBLE quotes expanded `$(...)` LOCALLY, so the "device" reading
(`uptime 427682s`, missing `/etc/openwrt_release`, `devmem: command not found`) was THIS HOST, not the
router - a confident wrong answer from an instrument that was never connected. Single-quote the remote
command so nothing expands before it reaches ssh.

### ★★★★ THE WALL, MEASURED END TO END (fire `ecwalk`, 2026-10-16)

UBI's own `ubi_io_read_ec_hdr()` acceptance test was run over the first 32 PEBs of **mtd13 (`rootfsa`)**
- the partition UBI is actually given - inside the stage-D hook, with the result carried out in the
tick's crumb. FIRED, read from the vendor:

    C18 = 0xC0DE502D
    C1C = 0x0A020016        writes=10, erases=2, EC passes = 0x00, attach code = 0x16

**EC passes = 0.** Not "some", not "a few": the walk stopped at the FIRST PEB. So the header our read
path hands UBI at byte 0 of mtd13 does not satisfy UBI's test, and `ubi_attach_mtd_dev()` refuses the
partition with -EINVAL because of it. (0 also results if `mtd_read()` itself refused - `got != 64`
takes the same `break` - so the next instrument must separate those two, see below.)

The chain is now measured at every link, not inferred:

    ubi.mtd=rootfsa in the effective cmdline   (built artifact + drivers/of/fdt.c:1065)      OK
    get_mtd_device_nm("rootfsa") resolves      (code was 0x16, not the 0x13 name failure)    OK
    ubi_attach_mtd_dev(mtd13, AUTO, 0, 0)      -> -EINVAL                                    MEASURED
    UBI's EC test over mtd13 PEB 0..31         -> 0 of 32 pass                               MEASURED

**This is the standing suspect in the record, finally confirmed by measurement rather than inference:**
"the remaining suspect is what OUR READ PATH hands UBI". The refusal is not in the attach's argument
checking (every explicit -EINVAL there was excluded by reading, and `vid_hdr_offset = 0` defaults to
`ALIGN(64, hdrs_min_io_size)` = 2048 on this geometry) - it is in the bytes.

### NEXT INSTRUMENT (one fire, and it must separate three worlds)

Encode into the tick crumb, from a read of mtd13 PEB 0 through the mtd layer at 64 bytes:

  1. whether `mtd_read()` itself succeeded and `got == 64` (vs. refused) - the 0 is ambiguous today
  2. a FIELD code for which test failed: magic / version byte / vid_hdr_offset / data_offset /
     EC counter / CRC
  3. the first four bytes as read, so the magic can be compared against 0x55424923 ("UBI#") literally

Highest-value single datum: the four raw bytes at offset 0 of mtd13. If they are not `55 42 49 23`,
the read path is delivering the wrong page (or an offset splice); if they ARE, the failure is in a
field or the CRC and the remaining candidates are `vid_hdr_offset != 2048`, `data_offset != 4096`, or
the CRC seed - and `LUOFU_UBI_CRC32_INIT` is one of the two constants this project has already got
wrong once ("a remembered constant is a hypothesis; the artifact outranks it").

Reference for what the bytes SHOULD be: an independent dump of this same partition showed 120 valid
EC headers (magic 0x55424923, version 1, vid_hdr_offset 2048, data_offset 4096, ec 0, CRC correct
against `crc32(seed, hdr, 60)` with UBI's non-inverting crc32).

### ★★★★ ROOT CAUSE OF THE ROOTFS WALL - OUR READ PATH RETURNS ZEROS (fire `ec2`, 2026-10-16)

The EC walk was extended to report WHICH test failed and the literal first bytes read. The fire's slot
write and priming succeeded; the readback was lost to a network blip on the host, and recovered for
free afterwards because the crumb persists:

    C18 = 0xC0DE50F1      low byte 0xF1 = THE MAGIC TEST FAILED (not 0xF0, the read-refused code)
    C1C = 0x0A020000      writes=10, erases=2, h[0]=0x00, h[1]=0x00

**Read plainly: `mtd_read()` over mtd13 PEB 0 SUCCEEDS and hands back 64 bytes whose first two are
`00 00`.** The flash there provably contains `55 42 49 23` ("UBI#") - an independent dump of this same
partition showed 120 valid EC headers. So the driver reports a successful read while delivering a
ZERO-FILLED page, and `ubi_attach_mtd_dev()` refuses the partition with -EINVAL because the EC magic it
reads is `00000000`.

**This is the whole rootfs wall, and it is one link below where every previous probe was aimed.** UBI
can never attach while our read path returns zeros, regardless of the command line, the initcall
order, the partition name, or the parameter.

It also closes two older suspicions with measurement:
  * `[[cudy-wr3000v2/fmc-erase-vs-program-split]]` recorded that **erase reaches the array but the data
    path does not** - now confirmed in the READ direction as well.
  * the log line `rootfs_data is mtd15 ... read=0 got=8: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` was read as "the
    partition is erased, and our path returns 0x00 for erased flash". It is better explained by the
    simpler statement: **our read path returns 0x00, full stop.** mtd13 is NOT erased and still reads 0.

### THE ONE REMAINING AMBIGUITY, AND THE FIRE THAT SETTLES IT

Two worlds produce "zeros at offset 0 of mtd13":

  (a) the READ PATH is dead and returns zeros for every page, everywhere; or
  (b) the read path is fine and mtd13's PARTITION BASE OFFSET is wrong, so "offset 0 of rootfsa"
      lands on unwritten flash (which this path returns as 0x00). `[[cudy-wr3000v2/fmc-partition-offset-bug]]`
      records two false fixes in exactly this area, so it is a live candidate.

**Next fire, decisive and cheap:** read offset 0 of three partitions IN THE SAME BOOT and put the first
two bytes of each into the crumb - `mtd11` (kernela) and `mtd12` (kernelb) hold known content (our
uImage, magic `0x27051956` = "\x27\x05\x19\x56"; kernelb holds the build just fired), and `mtd13`
is the question. If kernelb also reads `00 00`, the READ PATH is dead (world a). If kernelb returns
`27 05`, the read path works and rootfsa's offset arithmetic is wrong (world b). One per-partition crumb
cannot carry three answers, so use the step byte for WHICH partition and the payload for its bytes, and
run the same fire three times against the same image - or better, encode a single 6-bit field: 2 bytes
from kernelb in the payload, and a pass/fail byte for rootfsa in the step.

Reference for what a correct read must produce: `mtd11`/`mtd12` begin with the uImage magic
`0x27051956`, and the vendor kernel reading the same partitions reports real content - so the expected
bytes are known independently of our driver.

PROCESS: the fire's readback failed with "No route to host" because the host lost internet mid-run; the
device itself was fine and its crumb survived. When a readback fails on the HOST side, the measurement
is not lost - re-read it instead of re-firing.

A crumb payload `(flag<<24)|(vols<<16)|(kb0<<8)|(ra0)` was built and fired (slice md5 9eb5e490).
Readback: **C18 = 0xC0DE502D, C1C = 0x0A000000** - flag 0x0A (the EC self-check saw mtd13 NOT read
as 55 42), byte1 = 0x00 = **`ubi_attach_mtd_dev(mtd13, -1, 0, 0)` returned SUCCESS.**

That collides head-on with earlier fire `attach` (C1C = 0x0A026A16, the SAME call -EINVAL) on a
partition whose EC header is valid. And the seed of that collision is in the code that had been
staged for this session: `ubi_attach_mtd_dev()` was called **without `ubi_devices_mutex`**, which
build.c:833-835 says every caller must hold. An attach that returns 0 for a partition the kernel's
own ubi_init attached successfully is not evidence - it is a second attach mutating live state.

The `vols` fire's boot also went dark on BOTH addresses for ~75 s, then returned on the vendor with
the selector 0x11 (the fires' 0x11 gives up to the box's own fallback).

**AND THE TICK'S WRITE IS NOT THE LAST WORD.** `luofu_fmc_crumb()` lives at the top of the tick, but
the tick goes on: `ubi_read` -> `dev_info` -> the pstore block every 5 s. On a boot that SURVIVES,
the write that lands in C18/C1C is whichever tick's crumb ran last before the reset. On a boot that
does not survive, only the ladder's crumbs are there. So a C1C from a surviving boot is a
LAST-TICK sample, not a final report - read it that way or pin the answer to a level that runs once.

### WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED, STATED AS THE NEXT STEP

**Does the kernel replay `ubi.mtd` onto the built-in UBI module at all?** It is proven to reach
`unknown_bootoption` (a MODULE parameter: `module_param_call(mtd, ...)` is not a `__setup`, and its
symbol lives in `__modparam_`, not `__param_obs`), and it is proven NOT to be in `/proc/cmdline` on
the vendor (which runs a different kernel, so that is not evidence about ours). What is unmeasured is
whether `load_module()`'s replay calls `ubi_mtd_param_parse()` - one readable value decides it:
`mtd_devs` in the built-in `ubi` module right after `do_initcalls()`. That needs a hook that runs
BEFORE ubi_init (a device_initcall can read the built-in module's long section) and a crumb the
ladder already provides. This session could not build it: it is the same kind of static access the
lock-free attach already cost.

### INSTRUMENT DOCTRINE, ADDED TO THIS SESSION'S BILL

  1. I staged an instrument that attaches a live UBI device without its documented lock, and the
     box went dark on the first flight. "Read-only with respect to the system" (2026-10-16's rule)
     does not cover it: a call with documented concurrency requirements is a WRITER even when it
     looks like a query.
  2. The gate script's first version compared 3 hex chars to 8 and REFUSED a healthy partition.
     A gate that can only ever refuse is a bug; validate a parser against a known-good read before
     believing its refusal.
  3. Two WSL builds were started while a fire was in flight. They race the kernel build rather than
     the device, so nothing was harmed - but the 2026-10-16 rule (built tree vs source tree) plus one
     fire at a time is the cheaper discipline.
  4. The `vols` fire's log had no `boot_id AFTER` at the moment the first readback was attempted; the

     field as a failed fire - re-read the log.

## 2026-10-18 .. 2026-10-22 - the log channel, UBI's verdict, and the read-path wall

**PHASE 113 (10-18): the program opcode, measured live.** Sampling `0x10a20030` during a vendor
`mtd write` gave the literal pair: read `0x9A1`, erase `0x810`, program `0x9D0` - the hardware
expands compact inputs; the packed `0x9D1` was one dummy cycle too many. The `0x9D0` fire changed
the vendor's planted bytes in mtd9 PEB0: the program reached the array for the first time.

**PHASE 114 (10-19): the cell control, and the web-UI shell lane.** The C10/C14 poison did not
survive a vendor boot: the vendor writes both cells every boot (`0x02000000` / `0xDFDF0781`), so
every cell-based reading of the program path is withdrawn. The web UI restores a root shell on
factory-reset stock: wizard login (`sha256(pw+salt)` then `sha256(h1+token)`), then the `systime`
payload carrying BOTH `cbid.system.ntp.current` and `timeclock` (urlencoded; `timeclock` alone is
ignored), then `dropbearkey` (the shipped host keys are 0 bytes).

**PHASE 115 (10-21): the vendor write path, disassembled, and the log channel opened.**
`hi_flash.ko` (full symbols) gives the raw-NAND/SPI-NAND sequences: the program sets `OP_CFG=0x50`,
a plain `OP_CTRL=3`, a separate 0xff-filled OOB buffer, and no write-enable. Fired against our
driver: the vendor-literal build erased but did not program; the `0x9D0` + command-injection build
with the OOB destination fixed (`dma_buf + 0x2000`, not `+page_size`) **wrote the log** - page 0 plus
the ring pages from `0x800`. The captured ring then named the boot's killer:
`pstore_blk.best_effort=1` re-added by `build/tmp/wsl_build_kernel.sh` faults at 5.76 s; removed, the
boot reaches the rootfs mount. With `LUOFU_LOG_KEEP` at 15 KiB the ring reads UBI's verdict:

    5.909 ubi0: attaching mtd14
    6.086 ubi0: scanning is finished
    6.090 ubi0 error: ubi_read_volume_table: the layout volume was not found
    6.097 ubi_attach_mtd_dev: failed to attach mtd14, error -22
    6.520 VFS: Cannot open root device "ubiblock0_0" ... error -6

**PHASE 116 (10-22): the read path is the fault.** READ4/TREAD: every page reads zero with the
correct row (`ADDRL=0x6a800000` = mtd14's offset), `FMC_CFG=0x1823` (vendor-identical), the SFC gate
on and the reset deasserted - and `dma_buf[0] = 0`: the DMA never writes the buffer. Gating the
snapshot did not change it (poisoning rejected); `DMA_ATTR_FORCE_CONTIGUOUS` did not move the address
and changed the boot shape (reverted). Leading hypothesis: the box is **SPI-NAND**, and the read
writes the parallel-NAND literal `OP_CFG=0x50` where the SPI encoding is the packed `0x9A1` the live
vendor register showed. Reference: U-Boot `hifmc100_spi_nand.c`. Details:
`fmc-read-path-degradation-2026-10-21.md`, `fmc-vendor-write-path-2026-10-21.md`.

**PHASE 117 (10-22): the audit.** The 31-lane percentage model is retired as the headline (three
copies disagreed: 68/45/56 vs 70/50/58 vs the JSON). The live metric is the gate table in
`STATE.md`: G1 25 / G2 0 / G3 0. The structural audit is `AUDIT-2026-10-22.md`.


**PHASE 118 (10-30): the flash path comes alive, and the killer is ours.** Five defects, each
hiding the next. (1) **The DTB was never appended** - `CONFIG_ARM_APPENDED_DTB=y` but every packaging
script ran `mkimage -d arch/arm/boot/zImage` with nothing appended, so every DTS edit this project
ever made was compiled and discarded; the kernel booted the vendor's tree. Fixed (assert
`combined == zImage + dtb`), which moved the boot 70 s -> 310 s and let the initcall tower complete.
(2) **The DTS topology starved the flash probe**: `0x14880000` was split into the vendor's
`crg@`/`clk@` shape, but the vendor has TWO drivers and this tree has ONE - `luofu-crg` builds its
gates by walking its own children - so no clock provider existed, `devm_clk_get("sfc_clk")` returned
`-EPROBE_DEFER`, and `luofu_fmc_probe` **never ran**. Receipt: `C18 = 0xC0DE50FF`, `C1C = 0xC0DE5FFF`.
(3) **The CRG registered zero clocks**: `if (bank >= i)` compared the bank against the GATE INDEX,
and `i` is reset to 0 just above, so `0 >= 0` skipped every gate; plus the 16 gate children were
absent from the DTS entirely. Receipt: `C94 = 0xC0DE6003` (the GMAC receiving 3 clocks).
(4) **The reset provider had no `of_xlate`**: `reset_controller_register()` forces
`of_reset_n_cells = 1` when a controller supplies none, overriding the driver's 2, while every node
passes TWO cells - so every lookup tripped `WARN_ON(args_count != n_cells)` and returned `-EINVAL`.
(5) **THE KILLER: an unreserved fixed-address log ring.** `LUOFU_LOG_BASE = 0x80602000`, size
`0x4000`, is inside the DT memory node (`0x80500000 + 0x7b00000`), `__va()`'d into kernel memory and
written with up to 16 KiB of kernel log by `luofu_kmsg_to` - with **no `memblock_reserve` anywhere**.
To memblock it was free RAM just below the kernel image at `0x80608000`, so it overwrote whatever the
allocator placed there. That is why six driver bisects all returned identical results: the watchdog,
GMAC, MDIO, smccc, pl353 and LEDs were never the fault, only downstream. Disabling the ring
(`luofu_log_b = NULL`; every writer already null-guards) moved the boot from `t=70s` dying in
`device_initcall` to `t=310s` with **level 7 reached** - `C8C = 0x80604000` =
`virt_to_phys(swapper_pg_dir)` and `C9C = 0x80C837E8`, both primed to `0x55555555` first.
`luofu-gmac.c:565` carries a second hardcoded copy at `0x80603000`, inside the same window - still
live in the shipping config.

**Where the wall is now - and it is the original one.** With every initcall completing,
`ubi_read_volume_table` fails: `C18 = 0xC0DE5247` means `ubiblock0_0` did not resolve. UBI's own test
is `ubi_find_av(ai, UBI_LAYOUT_VOLUME_ID)` (id `0x7fffefff`); when the scan found valid PEBs but no
layout volume, it returns `-EINVAL`. The 2026-10-21 "reads zeros at 0x800" finding **does not
reproduce** on a working boot: a level-7 probe through the MTD layer returned `C18 = 0xC0DE52A0` -
partition `rootfsb` found by name, EC magic `UBI#`, `vid_hdr_offset` exactly `0x800`, and
`PEB0+0x800` reading `'U'`. So the read path, the addressing and the EC header are all correct; what
remains is the VID header's content (CRC / `vol_id`) or the partition offset itself.

**Instrument lessons, paid for in fires.** A cell that is not primed is not evidence: an unprimed
`C94` carried a previous boot's GMAC crumb and produced two contradictory conclusions, and an
unprimed `C8C` nearly produced a false "level 7 reached". `C04` is **vendor-zeroed** and cannot hold
an answer. `C18` is the one cell proven to survive a primed write. Verify a constant in the
**artifact** before spending a fire (`objdump | grep <literal>`), not by grepping the source for a
symbol name - a `static __init` helper is inlined and its name never appears. And two measurements
that disagree are a question about the instrument before the hardware.

## 2026-11-08 - the U-Boot abort key is not the gate; the serial RX path is

**Root, live env, and dumps.** The Cudy web UI accepts the setup password `<ROUTER-WEB-PASSWORD>` with the
page's own hash: `sha256(password + salt)`, then `sha256(h1 + token)` when a token field is present.
The authenticated systime page still executes the `date -s '%s'` injection as `uid=0(root)`. With
root, the live U-Boot environment, `/proc/mtd`, both U-Boot slots, and `bdinfo` were dumped. The
environment now carries `bootdelay=3`, `bootdelaykey=x`, and `bootstopkey=x`; the change was made
through a `/tmp/fw_setenv` symlink to `/bin/fw_printenv`, and `fw_printenv` reads it back.

**The keyed abort is measured dead.** Two captures on `/dev/ttyUSB0`:

- `bootdelay=30` (which the loader printed as `bootdelay is 48000`): 953 `x` bytes over 40 s,
  no abort, Linux booted.
- `bootdelay=3`: 522 `x` bytes sent continuously from before the U-Boot banner through
  `input <abort key> to stop autoboot in  1s`; the loader still printed
  `Reading 8650752 byte(s)` and booted.

U-Boot's stock `passwd_abort()` compares the **last N characters** of the input buffer against
`bootdelaykey`/`bootstopkey` and does not require Enter, so extra keys cannot break the match.
The key string is therefore ruled out. The U-Boot device tree has a `uart1@0x1010f000` node with
no `pinctrl-0` property, and the pinctrl node has no UART state, so the loader does not mux the
console RX pad; Linux's pinctrl does, which is why input echoes only after boot. **The U-Boot
prompt is not reachable by serial on this unit, and writing `bootstopkey`/`bootdelaykey` cannot
change that.** Side finding: the loader parses `bootdelay` as hex, so `bootdelay=30` became
48,000 ms; use a hex value (for example `1e`) for a 30 s delay.

**bdinfo decrypt fixed at the tool.** The live `mtd6` partition starts with a 4-byte header
(`00 00 00 01`) before the DES-CBC ciphertext, and the key is OpenSSL's `DES_string_to_key`
(MIT krb4), not the RFC 3961 variant the old helper implemented. The old helper decrypted from
offset 0 with the wrong key and produced garbage on a real dump; it only passed its synthetic
fixture. `tools/decrypt_bdinfo.py` now trims the `0xff` tail, tries offsets 0/4/8/12/16, scores
for `board =` plus `BDINFO_END`, and parses the text up to the NUL terminator. Re-run against the
live dump: offset 4, 56,834 bytes, fields include `board=WR3000`, `model=WR3000 V2.0`,
`country/region=US`, `deviceid=cudydevice`, MAC, serial, uuid, hmac, fuuid, and the 32-character
`secret`. The secret stays out of tracked text.

**Local dumps (gitignored, not in the repo):** `dumps/router-20261108/{uboota,ubootb,bdinfo,enva}.bin`,

remaining blocker is physical: sending Enter returns a single `0xFD` noise byte instead of
reaching the tty, so the FT232 TX line is not driving the router RX. That same dead path explains
the U-Boot key flood. Fixing the TX/RX wiring should make Enter activate `ash --login` (root).

## 2026-11-08 (later) - CVE-2026-71960 confirmed on the live Mosquitto broker

**The forged JWT works.** The router runs Mosquitto on 1883 (plain, JWT auth) and 8883 (TLS,
client certificate) with `allow_anonymous false` and `auth_plugin /usr/lib/auth_plugin_jwt.so`.
The ACL uses usernames `cudydevice` and `admincudydevice` and the 12-digit device ID
`000000000000`; the factory bdinfo `deviceid` is the placeholder `cudydevice`. A JWT forged from
the bdinfo `secret` with `--deviceid 000000000000` (username
`admincudydevice-000000000000`) got `CONNACK rc=0` and subscribed `router/#`; the broker log
records `clients: hb-research connected`. This is the live-device confirmation of
CVE-2026-71960.

**The command half is not demonstrable on this single unit.** `/var/run/cmagent` contains only
`000000000000`, and the device runs as the admin/controller (`/usr/sbin/cmagent ... -a`).
`sync_command` skips the controller ID, so there is no satellite to command. A publish to
`router/000000000000/000000000000/router/command` with `{"cmd":"id"}` was accepted by the broker
but not executed. Flipping `cmagent.mqtt.admin=0` started the satellite agent (no `-a`), but it
spent the window reinitializing Wi-Fi and did not process the command; the role was restored to
`admin=1`, the cmagent is back with `-a`, and the router is healthy (2 wiphys, 6 interfaces,
calibration SUCC, hostapd hashes unchanged). CVE-2026-71961 needs a real second mesh node (a
satellite) or a deeper trace of the satellite-mode subscription before it can be claimed.

## 2026-11-08 (later still) - CVE-2026-71961 proven; UBI read-path source regression

**The paragraph above is superseded.** The command chain runs on this single unit. The topic
contract is `<prefix>/<dst_did>/<src_did>/<seq>/<app>/<event>`, prefix `router`, handler
`/usr/lib/lua/cmagent/<app>/<event>.lua`. `command.lua` decodes the JSON payload and calls
`io.popen` on the `cmd` field only when `src_did` equals `000000000000`; it does not authenticate
the payload and does not quote the command.

The ACL correction: `auth_plugin_jwt.so` `acl_check` at `0x3310` returns
`MOSQ_ERR_PLUGIN_DEFER` (17), so `/etc/mosquitto/aclfile.conf` is enforced. The users are exact:
`cudydevice` reads `router/+/000000000000/+/+/+` and writes `router/000000000000/+/+/+/+`;
`admincudydevice` reads `router/000000000000/+/+/+/+`, writes `router/+/000000000000/+/+/+`, and
reads `$SYS/#`. The 12-digit `000000000000` is the controller sentinel in the topic, not the
bdinfo deviceid; the factory `deviceid` is `cudydevice`. The earlier
`admincudydevice-000000000000` attempt authenticated, but the exact ACL `user` did not match, so
`router/#` was not a granted subscription.

The live chain: a forged HS256 token with MQTT username and `username` grant `cudydevice` got
CONNACK rc=0. Publishing `router/000000000000/000000000000/7/router/command` with
`{"cmd":"id > /tmp/omo-71961-verify.txt","reply":1}\x00` executed as root. The trailing NUL is
required by the C JSON sniff (`payload[payloadlen-2] == '}'`); bare JSON takes the AES-decrypt
path and fails with `Expected value but found invalid token at character 1`. The admin's own
`router/000000000000/+/+/+/+` subscription receives the message, and `command.lua` trusts
`src_did=000000000000` and calls `io.popen` as root. The file read `uid=0(root) gid=0(root)`; the
log showed `shell cmd id > /tmp/omo-71961-verify.txt`; the reply was
`{"message":"success","data":"","code":0}` on `.../router/reply`. The subagent's `id-final` run
and the parent's `id-verify` run both succeeded; no second node was used. Evidence:
`dumps/router-20261108/mqtt-command-chain-report.md` and `evidence/`. The router stayed at 2
wiphys, 6 interfaces, `admin=1`, cmagent `-a`, no `.omo-off`; the temp files were removed; no Wi-Fi
command, role change, or reboot.

The kernel UBI report (`dumps/router-20261108/ubi-readpath-report.md`) finds the ECC-off page-tail
loss: `luofu-fmc.c:127` has `luofu_read_ecc_off = true`; `DMA_LEN = 1` bounds each transfer to
2048 bytes including the 14-byte spare splice at offset 1040, so page offsets 2034..2047 come
back zero. The 11-page volume table's record 118 CRC field (page 9 offset 2032..2035) reads
`f1160000` instead of `f116c36b`; `vtbl_check()` rejects both layout copies and `process_lvol()`
returns `-EINVAL`. The host simulation on `mtd13-rootfsa.bin` reproduces exactly one bad record,
118; the `mtd13` and `mtd14` volume tables are byte-identical. The dumped `kernelb.vmlinux` is a
raw Image (base `0xc0608000`); at `0xc092215c` it calls `luofu_fmc_ecc_type_get`, passes the saved
type to `luofu_fmc_ecc_type_set` (no `mov r1, #0`), and does one `mmiocpy` with
`spec.page_size` at `0xc092239c`. The flashed binary is the ECC-on plain-copy shape; the tracked
source is the stale ECC-off copy. The one-line `luofu_read_ecc_off = false` fix plus the report's
comment is applied in the submodule; it is not compiled here (no ARM cross-gcc, no
`/opt/kbuild/linux-5.10.201`, no WSL). The next check is the live `rootfsb` (`ubi.mtd=rootfsb`)
and the UART-free `C9C`/`C18`/pstore/MTD readback plan in the report.

The writeup `gist-cudy-wr3000v2-mqtt-jwt.md` was corrected to the proven chain and the enforced
ACL; `tools/forge_jwt.py` and `tools/mqtt_takeover.py` now use the exact ACL roles, the six-field
topic, and the trailing-NUL payload. No secret or token is in tracked text.

## 2026-11-08 - C94 ladder: the kernel reaches the init hand-off and kernel_execve returns

The userspace-handoff ladder in `init/main.c` was built into the XZ full slice and fired once
from a fresh flash. Markers: `0x9B01` at `kernel_init_freeable` start, `0x9B02` before
`prepare_namespace`, `0x9B03` after it, `0x9B04` at function end, `0x9B05` before the init
attempts, `0x9B06/07/08` around `run_init_process` and `kernel_execve`.

The box ran ~36 s and failed over to vendor A. `C94 = 0xC0DE9B08`: every marker through the
return of `kernel_execve` ran. So:

- all late initcalls completed (`0x9A01` before the ladder);
- `prepare_namespace()` returned (`0x9B03`);
- `kernel_init_freeable()` returned (`0x9B04`);
- `run_init_process()` was entered (`0x9B06`), reached `kernel_execve` (`0x9B07`), and the
  call returned (`0x9B08`).

The hang/reset is after the last init attempt returns, not inside the exec. The likely failure
is the init itself returning `-ENOENT` (the mounted root has no `/sbin/init` or its interpreter)
or another exec error, followed by the panic path hanging until the watchdog. The next marker
should record `0xC0DE9B00 | (ret & 0xff)` and, if needed, the `mount_root` result. The known-good
control reached `C9C = 0x015EB70F` (`run_init_process` returned 0), so its init started; this
difference is the rootfs/init, not the early kernel.

Fresh-flash requirement confirmed: a second boot of the same slice without re-flashing failed
fast. The failover writes four zero bytes at the first byte after the slice (offset 2,707,196);
with that status present, `bootfip` rejects the image in ~9 s. Re-flashing the full slice restores
the ~36 s kernel run. Every fire must re-flash.

The console reader at `/dev/ttyUSB0` still receives only NUL bytes (57 in the last capture, no
ASCII). Pin 4 is readable per the user, but the adapter is not seeing the console; the cell
channel is the reliable one.

Box after the fire: vendor slot A, `bootflag=a`, `boot_reg=0x10`, uptime 69 s, Wi-Fi
`Cudy-1C73` / `Cudy-1C73-5G` up. `mtd12` holds the stage-2 slice (md5
`f2286c7a46cf4a0c4ad4f045bfc18fa8`, 2,707,252 B). The pre-fire known-good partition remains
the dump. The TFTP door is armed.


## 2026-11-08 - CORRECTION and milestone: kernel_execve returns 0, userspace starts

The `0x9B08` marker in the previous section only meant "the call returned"; it did not carry
the return code. The next fire replaced it with `0xC0DE9B00 | (ret & 0xff)` and read
`C94 = 0xC0DE9B00`, so the low byte is zero and `kernel_execve` returned 0. The init process
started. Every marker before it ran: all late initcalls (`0x9A01`), `prepare_namespace`
(`0x9B02/03`), `kernel_init_freeable` (`0x9B04`), `run_init_process` (`0x9B06/07`), and the
exec returned successfully. The known-good control's `C9C = 0x015EB70F` says the same thing.

The box still resets at ~36 s, with `C1C = 0xC0DE5E05` (the tick's 35.89 s mark). The remaining
failure is in userspace, most likely the overlay/rootfs setup and the watchdog hand-off: the
kernel's init hands the watchdog fd to procd, and procd has not reached the point where it pets
it. The known-good control resets later (~66 s), so its userspace gets further. The next
diagnostic is a kernel-side watchdog pet (the project's documented debugging shim) or a longer
watchdog timeout, to keep the box alive long enough to inspect userspace and the network.

The UART reader still receives only NUL bytes; pin 4 is readable per the user, but no console
ASCII arrives. The cells remain the reliable channel. Fresh-flash-before-every-boot is still
required (the failover writes four zero bytes after the slice).


## 2026-11-08 - the watchdog wall is broken; the box now survives to ~98 s, and the wall moves to userspace

A bounded pet timer was added to `mach-luofu/luofu.c`: every 5 s it writes the vendor's own
clear sequence (`reset-val0` then `reset-val1` to the watchdog clr-offset `0x14880070`) and
stops after 18 beats (90 s). This is a diagnostic shim, not a driver.

Result: the box did not fail over at ~36 s. It stayed down through t=130 s and the vendor
returned at t=140 s with uptime 41.6 s, i.e. the vendor boot began at about 98 s. The last pet
was at ~85 s and the hardware timeout is ~15 s (the vendor's live `set-offset` decodes to 15 s,
not 30 s), so the reset at ~98-100 s is exactly the expected post-pet expiry. **The 36 s reset
was the hardware watchdog, and the pet breaks past it.**

The cells after the failover: `C94 = 0xC0DE9B00` (the init started; unchanged), `C1C =
0xC0DE5E05` (the FMC tick's last value is still the 35.89 s mark, so C1C is not a kernel-alive
clock - the pet timer itself ran to 90 s). The box was alive for ~60 s longer than before the
shim, and during that time **no SSH, no Ethernet, and no userspace service appeared**. The
next wall is therefore userspace: the init process starts, but the rootfs/overlay/network
hand-off does not reach a point where the box is reachable. The persistent overlay remains the
known failure (`rootfs_data` block 0 reads `ff`, `volume_identify` returns `FS_NONE`, tmpfs
fallback), and G4 Ethernet is still one defect from green.

The pet is bounded so a broken userspace cannot strand the bench on our kernel; the vendor
returned on its own. The source change is in `opensource/lab/luofu-kernel/mach-luofu/luofu.c`
(and the build-tree copy). The next experiment should either lengthen the pet and try to reach
a userspace/network marker, or attack the overlay `volume_identify` path. The UART reader still
receives only NULs.

Box: vendor slot A, `bootflag=a`, `boot_reg=0x10`, uptime 70 s, Wi-Fi up. `mtd12` holds the
pet slice (md5 `4d320c5af5b9f756e80dc74f976abf84`). The pre-fire known-good partition remains
the dump. The TFTP door is armed.


## 2026-11-08 - RECOVERY: the RESET-hold TFTP door restored the box

The writable-MTD fire stranded the box: no return in 200 s. The RESET hold in the hung kernel
did nothing (the button is Linux userspace). The power-on hold with the cable on the WAN port
triggered the bootloader door. The first attempt failed because the host had lost the
`192.168.1.88` alias and UFW was dropping inbound UDP; after restoring the alias on
`enp195s0f3u1` and allowing `69/udp`, the U-Boot fetched `recovery.bin` and the server logged
`RRQ sent 20975775 bytes`. The box is back: `192.168.10.1` answers HTTP 200 with the vendor
2.4.15 web UI. SSH is refused, so dropbear is not up (factory-reset or stopped); use the web
UI to set the root password and start dropbear, then set `bootflag=a` and `boot_reg=0x10` to
leave slot A.

The lesson is recorded in STATUS: do not bind the FMC `_write`/`_erase` hooks or set
`MTD_WRITEABLE` until a single-page kernel-side write test on `upgrade` logs a cell result.
The write path is not proven in this build.

control r0 it captured. The kernel entry ran through stext and the page tables and died before the
MMU turned on. C20/C24/C28 read 1 (those offsets are not writable), so they carry nothing.

calibrated for the 6d904f5 image. Removing the write test shrank the image by 1,592 bytes and shifted
that address, so the reader treated code as a descriptor and faulted before the mcr. The uImage
payload/trailer shift is NOT the blocker: the kernel entry itself ran. The reader is removed in the
build tree; the 0xC0DE0017 breadcrumb and its captured r0 stay.

boot). Any boot that can reach the initcalls still needs the 600 s window.

## 2026-11-09 - SCAN DEPTH: C98=0x9A000006 - stalls at the eraseblock entry, before the data read

The scan-depth build returned C98=0x9A000006 (jffs2_scan_eraseblock entry), C88 at the UBI count,
C18=0xC0DE50E5. The driver deliberately sets the rootfs_data partition's oobsize/oobavail to 0, so
jffs2_cleanmarker_oob() is false and mtd_block_isbad/the OOB cleanmarker read are skipped; the stall
is at the in-band data read, i.e. jffs2_flash_read -> mtd_read on the partition.

Crumbs now: 0x9A000007 at jffs2_flash_read entry, 0x9A000008 after down_read(&c->wbuf_sem), and
0x9A000009 at the FMC driver's luofu_mtd_read entry. The last value names the layer: 0x9A08 means the
wbuf read lock or the mtd core before the driver, 0x9A09 the driver entry before the page read, and
0x9C... means the page read itself ran.

## 2026-11-09 - READ BOUNDARY: C98=0x9A000006 - the cleanmarker OOB path is the wall

The boundary build returned C98=0x9A000006 and no 0x9A07 (jffs2_flash_read never called). The stall is
inside jffs2_scan_eraseblock's cleanmarker block. The root cause is in fs/jffs2/os-linux.h:111:

    #define jffs2_cleanmarker_oob(c) (c->mtd->type == MTD_NANDFLASH)

It ignores the driver's deliberate part->oobsize/oobavail = 0, so the scan calls
jffs2_check_nand_cleanmarker -> mtd_read_oob on a device with no _read_oob, gets -EOPNOTSUPP, and the
mount fails (the driver's own comment quotes the -95 error). The driver set oobavail=0 and wrote an
in-band cleanmarker at partition page 0 for exactly this case, but the macro's type-only test defeats
it.

Fix: require oobavail in the macro, so a no-OOB NAND partition uses the in-band cleanmarker:
    #define jffs2_cleanmarker_oob(c) (c->mtd->type == MTD_NANDFLASH && c->mtd->oobavail)
Then the scan must proceed to jffs2_flash_read, and the FMC rows in mtd15 (0x9900+) will appear in C98.

## 2026-11-09 - NO-OOB FIX DID NOT CHANGE THE STALL; C98 still 0x9A000006

The macro change compiled (scan.o/fs.o/super.o/wbuf.o rebuilt) but the boot still left C98=0x9A000006
with no wbuf/flash read. That means jffs2_cleanmarker_oob(c) was still true at runtime, i.e.

## 2026-11-10 - 1,638 vs 8,612 reads across boots at a constant 705 s: the scan is SLOW and the watchdog kills it

The culprit is the driver's per-page read path: spin_lock_irqsave around luofu_fmc_read_page, whose
completion poll is udelay-based and can run long, so interrupts (and the pet timer's softirq) are held
off page after page. The driver's own comment already warns that this exact pattern "is a way to starve
the timers" and that "the SoC watchdog is what finally resets the box".

Fix: take a plain spin_lock (IRQs stay on) around the shared page buffer, so the timer/pet runs while
the scan crawls. With the timer alive the 1800 s pet covers the ~10-15 min scan, and the mount can
finish instead of being cut off at 705 s.

plus the mount to finish, then let the watchdog reset back to the vendor so the cells can be read.
