## 2026-11-10 - Read speed lever: switch completion from INT_STATUS bit 0 to the vendor's OP_CTRL clear

The 73 ms/read is the FMC_CMD_POLLS loop (100,000 iterations, udelay(1)) waiting on INT_STATUS bit 0.
The driver's own comment records the vendor's completion order: "poll OP_CTRL (0x68) bit 0 until it
CLEARS <- the DMA completion" and notes the INT_STATUS-bit-0 protocol "let the copy run before the
engine had moved the page". Switching the wait to the vendor's OP_CTRL busy-clear should complete in
the engine's real time and cut the per-page cost enough for the ~800 s scan to fit the ~704 s window.

Next: change the read_page poll to OP_CTRL bit 0 clear, rebuild, fire, and compare C88 at the reset
(higher reads/s means the scan is fitting).

(CONFIG_OVERLAY_FS=y; kernel grew to 2.70 MB) but not yet exercised.

Both halves are individually mountable: jffs2 upper on rootfs_data, squashfs lower on rootfsa. The
remaining wall is assembling them: mount both, then mount "overlay" with lowerdir/upperdir/workdir
(userspace paths are the natural place for this). Then exercise a write through the overlay to test
the jffs2 wbuf path.

## 2026-11-10 - C94 verdict is overwritten by our own exec ladder; the ladder must publish it

Fire `step0` (slice built 14:12 +07, fired 14:13): the mount test's verdict was routed to a global that
the mach watchdog pet republishes to C94 every beat, plus an immediate C94 deposit. After the vendor
returned at +705 s, C94 still read 0xC0DE9B00, the init exec ladder's own value, while C88=0x9C00024D
(589 reads) proves the boot ran and reached the userspace jffs2 scan. So neither the mount test deposit
nor the pet beat is the last C94 writer in a boot: init/main.c's `luofu_stage(0xC0DE9B00 | ret)` runs
after the pet's last effective beat and overwrites the verdict.

Fix built as `step0b` (not yet fired): the exec site now writes `luofu_overlay_verdict` when the mount
test set one, and keeps `0xC0DE9B00|ret` for a failed exec. The change is in init/main.c only. Rebuild
verified in vmlinux: the ret==0 path loads 0xc0817a60 and the literal 0xc0de9b00, and `moveq` selects
the ladder value only when the verdict is zero.

Two side findings from the same fire:
- The userspace `/init` mark at mtd15 0xE0000 (a 4-byte code, written by init-raw.c) read back 0xff
  after the vendor boot. The vendor's own jffs2 mounts rootfs_data and garbage-collects that block, so
  the raw mark is not a durable cross-boot readout. The cell readout remains the path.
- The box returned healthy: 2 wiphys, 6 interfaces, calibration [SUCC], 0 .omo-off leftovers.

## 2026-11-10 - STEP 0 VERIFIED: C94=0xC0DE9D00, the mount test's verdict survives the vendor boot

Slice `step0b` (the exec ladder now publishes `luofu_overlay_verdict`) fired at 14:26 and the vendor
returned at 14:38:39. Cells: C94=0xC0DE9D00, C88=0x9C00024D (589 reads), C98=0x9E030044,
C18=0xC0DE50E5, C1C=0xC0DE4B01. This is the first verdict that is attributable to the mount test
rather than to the exec ladder.

The value means the mount test RAN and all three mounts failed (no bits set), which matches the source
exactly: the initramfs carries only `/init`, so `/overlay`, `/mnt/lower`, and `/mnt/new` do not exist
and init_mount() returns -ENOENT at kern_path() before reaching any filesystem.

The readout is now unambiguous:
- 0xC0DE9D0x: the mount test ran; bits 1/2/4 = jffs2 / squashfs / overlay mounted.
- 0xC0DE9B0x: exec failed with errno x, or the mount test never set a verdict and exec succeeded.
- 0x9f00xxxx: the pet ran, but no verdict was ever published (the mount test did not return).

Mechanism, now measured end to end: the mount test sets `luofu_overlay_verdict`; the mach pet
republishes it to C94 every beat; init/main.c's exec site writes the verdict instead of
`0xC0DE9B00|ret` when it is set. The exec ladder is the last C94 writer in a boot, which is why the
earlier pet-only fire could not survive.

Side finding confirmed again: the userspace `/init` mark at mtd15 0xE0000 is not durable across the
vendor boot (the vendor's jffs2 GC erases that block), so the sysctrl cells remain the readout.

whiteout probe). The overlay used the empty /mnt/lower directory as its lower because the squashfs
mount failed, so bit 4 alone is not evidence that the real lower was in place; only 0xC0DE9D07 is.

The squashfs failure is the SOURCE STRING. The call used `init_mount("mtd:rootfsa", ...)`; the

mount_bdev(), which needs a block device path. `/dev/mtdblock13` is not available either at this
point, because devtmpfs is only mounted in prepare_namespace(), AFTER late_initcall_sync.

Fix for `step1b`: create /dev, mount devtmpfs there from the test, and use /dev/mtdblock13 as the
squashfs source. Diagnostic bit 3 records a failed devtmpfs mount, so full success stays 0xC0DE9D07.

missing block node (errno 2) distinguishable from a rejected squashfs (errno 22) or a busy device
(errno 16). Full success remains 0xC0DE9D07.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE A DIAGNOSTIC: C94=0x9D16006D - headers read clean, vtbl record 118 does not

Fire `phase2a` added a metadata comparison to the failure verdict: read the EC header at 0, the VID
header at 2048, and vtbl record 118 at 24392 through our MTD path, and compare their trailing CRCs
with the vendor's exact values (65 62 45 3d, b8 25 64 a8, f1 16 c3 6b). Result: C94=0x9D16006D.
Bits 5 and 6 are set, so the EC and VID headers are byte-identical to the vendor's. Bit 7 is clear,
so vtbl record 118 is still corrupted. C88=0x9C00055C.

The driver's own comment on the ECC path names this exact failure: with the ECC engine OFF the
controller splices 14 spare bytes in at offset 1040, and record 118's CRC arrives as 0xf1160000
instead of 0xf116c36b. The read path restored `saved`, the FMC_CFG ECC_TYPE read at entry, instead of
forcing the vendor's ECC-on value. A prior erase/write path can leave ECC_TYPE at 0, so the read ran
with the engine off while taking the plain-copy branch. The vendor's live FMC_CFG is 0x1823,
ECC_TYPE = 1.

`phase2b` forces ECC type 1 for every data read and restores `saved` on the way out. The build shows
`mov r1, #1` before the `luofu_fmc_ecc_type_set` call in `luofu_fmc_read_page`. If this is the only
defect, the UBI attach should now pass vtbl_check, ubi_init's ubiblock creation should register
ubiblock0_0, and the mount test should reach 0xC0DE9D07.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE A BREAKTHROUGH: ECC on fixes record 118 and the UBI attach; the ubiblock node had a dev_t bug

Fire `phase2b` returned C94=0x9D0600E5 with C88=0x9C0020AC (8,364 reads, the full UBI attach scan).
Decoded: j1 ok, j3 ok, the ubiblock-lookup failure bit CLEAR (d = 0), and metadata bits 5, 6 and 7
ALL set. So forcing the vendor's ECC type 1 did exactly what the driver comment predicted: record
118's CRC now matches, vtbl_check passes, ubi0 attaches, and ubiblock0_0 exists. The UBI wall is down.

The only failure left was j2 = -ENXIO (6). That is the block-device open, not the data: the mount
node was created with `blk_lookup_devt()`'s kernel dev_t, but `init_mknod()` runs its third argument
through `new_decode_dev()`. The kernel dev_t is MKDEV(major << 20 | minor); new_decode_dev treats it
as the glibc new-encoding, produces the wrong major/minor, and the block layer has no disk for it.
Hence -ENXIO. `phase2c` passes `new_encode_dev(dt)` instead; the disassembly shows the shift/mask
encoding immediately before `init_mknod`.

If `phase2c` returns 0xC0DE9D07, Phase A (UBI attach and squashfs lower) and the overlay assembly's
three-mount target are both closed. The next wall is Phase B: a write through the overlay and the
jffs2 wbuf path.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B: C94=0x9E001E07 - the overlay create returns -EROFS

Fire `phase2e` returned C94=0x9E001E07. Tag 0x9E, status 0x07 (all three mounts up), errno 0x1E = 30,
which is -EROFS. The three mounts are stable, so the refusal is at the write layer: the overlay's
`filp_open(..., O_CREAT)` was rejected as a read-only filesystem before anything reached flash.

Two readings are consistent with the evidence:

  temp-file whiteout rename). If one of those writes fails inside jffs2's write buffer, jffs2 marks
  the superblock read-only, and the later create returns -EROFS even though the mount succeeded.
- The jffs2 superblock was already read-only but the overlay's upper check was satisfied by the mount
  record rather than the live flag; the create then hits the VFS read-only check.

The raw seed test erases and programs through `luofu_fmc_erase_block`/`luofu_fmc_write_page`
directly. jffs2 goes through `mtd_erase`/`mtd_write` and the `luofu_mtd_erase`/`luofu_mtd_write`
hooks, a path the current tree has not exercised in a fire. The next experiment is direct: erase and
program a free rootfs_data block through the MTD hooks and read it back through the raw FMC read
path, plus a `sb_rdonly()` check on the jffs2 and overlay superblocks at the moment of the failed
create. That separates a hook defect from a jffs2 superblock flip.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B DIAGNOSTIC 2: C94=0x9E401E27 - the MTD erase returned 0 but did not erase block 1

Fire `phase2g` returned C94=0x9E401E27. The hook code in bits 16-23 is 0x40: erase and write both
returned 0, and the readback differed. The low byte is unchanged (mounts 0x07, jffs2 rw, overlay sb
ro, errno 30).

The vendor's mtd16 at 0x20000 explains the mismatch exactly. The page still begins with the old
`HSPQ` firmware header, and our XOR pattern appears from offset 0x38 onward. On NAND a program can
only clear bits, and 0x48&0x5a=0x48, 0x53&0x5b=0x53, 0x50&0x58=0x50, 0x51&0x59=0x51: the old
header is the AND of the old bytes with our buffer. So `luofu_mtd_erase` WAS called, returned 0, and
left the block programmed; the write then programmed over it. The MTD erase hook is a silent no-op
on upgrade block 1, while the raw seed test's `luofu_fmc_erase_block` still works on rootfs_data.

Two candidates: block 1 is special (bad/protected/reserved in the BBT), or the erase hook's on-disk
effect differs from the raw call. `phase2h` moves the same hook test to upgrade block 2 (offset
0x40000), the block the earlier raw page-163 write test proved erasable and writable. If the hooks
pass there, block 1 was the anomaly; if they fail, the hook path is the defect.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B DIAGNOSTIC 3: C94=0x9E401E27 on block 2 too - the MTD erase hook no-ops

Fire `phase2h` moved the hook test to upgrade block 2 (offset 0x40000) and returned the same
C94=0x9E401E27. Hook code 0x40 again: erase returned 0, write returned 0, readback differed. Block 1
was not special. The raw page-163 write test on this same block erased it and programmed LUFU through
`luofu_fmc_erase_block`/`luofu_fmc_write_page`; the `mtd_erase` path is what fails to erase.

The erase hook computes `row = div_u64(mtd_get_master_ofs(mtd, pos), mtd->writesize)` and calls
`luofu_fmc_erase_block(fmc, row)`. The write hook uses the same translation and its program lands,
so the defect is specific to the erase path: either the hook receives a partition-relative address
and `mtd_get_master_ofs()` adds the partition base a second time (targeting a wrong, high row and
returning 0), or the erase call inside the hook differs from the raw call. The overwritten `HSPQ`
header at 0x20000 and the unchanged block-2 page both fit a wrong-row silent no-op.

Next experiment: on the same block, call `luofu_fmc_erase_block()` directly with the expected
master row and compare it with `mtd_erase()`; log `instr->addr`, the computed row and the erase
return in the verdict, so the address convention is measured rather than assumed. Then fix the hook
translation or the call.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B COMPARISON 3: 0x8E4040 on block 0 too - the read races the program

next wall.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B COMPARISON 4: 0x8E4040 persists with a 20 ms settle

Fire `phase2l` added `msleep(20)` between the program and the readback in both the raw and MTD paths
and still returned C94=0x8E4040. The timing hypothesis is dead: the readback is not racing tPROG, or
the readback itself reads something other than the programmed page. The erase and the program both
return 0, so the next thing to establish is what the page actually contains.

`phase2m` encodes the raw and MTD readback first bytes into the verdict: C94=0x8E40XXYY where XX is
the raw readback byte 0 and YY the MTD readback byte 0. The pattern's first byte is 0x5a, the seed's
first byte is 0x85, erased flash is 0xff, zeros are 0x00. That single byte distinguishes "the write
landed and the compare is wrong" from "the erase never happened" and "the program never landed".

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B COMPARISON 5: 0x8E400000 - zeros, and the write path never set ECC

Fire `phase2m` returned C94=0x8E400000: the raw code is 0x40 and BOTH readback first bytes are
0x00. Not the pattern (0x5a), not the seed (0x85), not erased flash (0xff). The reads succeeded and
returned zeros.

The driver explains it. `luofu_fmc_read_page()` forces the on-die ECC type to 1, but
`luofu_fmc_write_page()` never sets the ECC type at all: it inherits whatever the previous operation
left, and `luofu_fmc_erase_block()` restores its own entry value. So a program can go out with ECC
off while every read is type 1, and the page reads back as garbage or zeros. The seed test only
worked because its write happened to inherit type 1.

Fix applied: `luofu_fmc_write_page()` now saves the ECC type, sets type 1 before the program, and
restores it after, so the program and the read always agree. `phase2n` reruns the same block-0
comparison; a verdict of 0x8E00005A (raw code 0, readback 0x5a) would prove the write lands with the
read's ECC.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B COMPARISON 6: ECC was not it - the program operands are invalid

Fire `phase2n` with the explicit ECC type still returned C94=0x8E400000. The ECC hypothesis was
wrong, or at least not the whole defect. The answer was already in the C88 self-test: it encodes the
program's actual operands, and it has been reading 0x9C0020BD, which decodes to wr_cmd 0x00,
wr_if_type 1, wr_addr_cyc 0, wr_dummy 2. The bootloader spec record overrides the good defaults
(wr_cmd 0x32, if_type 3, addr_cyc 5, dummy 0) with zeroes. The write path puts wr_cmd into OP_CTRL
bits 8-15, so every program went out with command 0x00 and no address. Nothing was programmed, the
block stayed erased, and a read of the erased page returns zeros - which is exactly what phase2m
measured.

Fix applied: the write operands are pinned to the measured-good defaults (if_type 3, wr_cmd 0x32,
addr_cyc 5, dummy 0) after the record parse. `phase2o` reruns the block-0 comparison; the C88
self-test's wr_cmd field should read 0x32 and its mismatch count should fall to zero if the program
lands.

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B COMPARISON 7: the operands were dead code - the write hardcodes 0x9A0

Fire `phase2o` returned C94=0x8E400000 and C88=0x9C0020BD, unchanged. The pin changed nothing
because the write path computes an OP_CFG from the spec and then **overwrites it with a hardcoded
`0x9A0`**. The driver's own comments around that line name the symptom exactly: the 0x9A0 shape is
"accepted, array unchanged", and the earlier `0x9D0` shape "demonstrably reaches the array" - it is
the one behind the page-163 LUFU proof. The 0x9A0 was installed later on a re-reading of the
vendor's disassembly, and it is the regression.

Restored `op_cfg = 0x9D0u` in `luofu_fmc_write_page()`. The ECC pin and the spec pin stay (both are
correct and harmless), but the OP_CFG is now the proven shape. `phase2p` reruns the block-0
comparison; the raw code should go to 0 and the readback byte to 0x5a.

The OP_CFG 0x9D0 is right (the tracked driver's measured "PROGRAM 0x9D0"). What the path never

controller delivered nothing. That is the same stale-buffer behaviour the driver documented on
2026-10-14, and it means every in-kernel readback in this line of tests is untrustworthy unless a
vendor dd corroborates it.

So block 3 is good, the write still never lands on the mounted partition, and the lock question is
open. `phase2v` reads the NAND's feature status (0xA0) and config (0xB0) into the verdict - the
status byte carries the block-protection/lock bits - and then issues the per-block unlock (0x7f)
with the block's row address, in the erase command shape, before the same erase/write. The vendor

## 2026-11-10 - PHASE B ROOT CAUSE: the probe SETS the FMC write-protect the vendor clears

Fire `phase2v` returned C94=0x8E00005A: the status byte read from feature 0xA0 is 0x00, so the NAND
itself is not block-protected, and the per-block unlock changed nothing. The vendor dd of page 192 is
still all-0xff.

The answer was in the vendor module all along. `hi_flash.ko` has `hi_fmc_wp_en_set` /
`hi_fmc_wp_en_check` (bit 6 of `FMC_GLOBAL_CFG`) and `hi_nand_wp_enable` / `hi_nand_wp_disable`,
and its MTD erase prints "Device is write protected" when the bit is set. The vendor's driver clears
the bit before a write or erase and sets it after.

**Our probe does the opposite.** The line whose comment reads "clear the write-protect bit by hand,
 as the vendor does" is

    writel(readl(fmc->regs + FMC_GLOBAL_CFG) | BIT(6), fmc->regs + FMC_GLOBAL_CFG);

It ORs the bit in. Our driver has been turning the flash write protection ON at every boot and then
wondering why accepted programs leave the array untouched. Fixed: `& ~FMC_GCFG_WP_EN`. `phase2w`
reruns the rootfs_data block-3 write; the vendor dd of page 192 should finally show the pattern.

`wr` write test only runs when all three mounts are zero, so it never ran and the vendor's page 192
is still ff.

So the write-protect fix changed the boot in a different way: the seed test's erase and seed now
actually happen, the jffs2 mounts read-write, and the overlay mount is the next refusal. The failure
layout currently does not carry the j3 errno (it carries j1's and j2's), so `phase2x` swaps the j2
errno field for the j3's. The next verdict will name the overlay mount's error directly.

`phase2y` creates /overlay/upper and /overlay/work on the just-mounted jffs2 before the overlay

bits). The likely values are EROFS if the overlay superblock is read-only, EIO from the jffs2 write
path, or ENOSPC from the small partition. The raw/mtd byte pair stays as the secondary readout.

The kernel source names the reason. In fs/overlayfs/super.c the mount ends with:

    if (!ovl_force_readonly(ofs) && ofs->config.index) {
            err = ovl_get_indexdir(sb, ofs, oe, &upperpath);
            ...
            if (!ofs->indexdir)
                    sb->s_flags |= SB_RDONLY;

With the index feature enabled by default, a jffs2 upper that cannot host the index directory leaves
ofs->indexdir empty and the overlay is FORCED READ-ONLY - exactly the observed mount-ok, write-EROFS
pair. The jffs2 upper here does not provide that index directory.

`phase3a` mounts with `index=off`, which skips the block entirely. If the sb then comes up rw the
write test runs, and its success tag is 0xC0DE9D0F (the 0xC0DE9D00 base with the j1/j2/j3/wr bits).

`phase3b` reads both superblocks directly: kern_path("/overlay") is the jffs2, kern_path("/mnt/new")

a read-only jffs2 points at the MTD/JFFS2 mount, while a read-only overlay with a writable jffs2
points back into overlayfs's own workdir/index logic.

## 2026-11-12 - PHASE B ROOT CAUSE: 5.10 never gives jffs2 a write buffer on this MTD

The EINVAL is not jffs2's inode hash. It is this driver refusing the write jffs2 issues.

In 5.10, `fs/jffs2/os-linux.h` hardcodes `jffs2_cleanmarker_oob(c)` to 0, so `jffs2_nand_flash_setup()`
is never called and the write buffer is set up only by `jffs2_nor_wbuf_flash_setup()`, whose
predicate is `c->mtd->type == MTD_NORFLASH && !(c->mtd->flags & MTD_BIT_WRITEABLE)`. Our partitions
inherit `MTD_NANDFLASH` from the master, so that predicate is false:

- `jffs2_is_writebuffered(c)` is false,
- `jffs2_flash_writev()` takes `jffs2_flash_direct_writev()`,
- which hands `mtd_write()` the node's exact offset and length, e.g. a 0x44-byte dirent at 0x1d8,
- and `luofu_mtd_write()` is a page programmer: it returns -EINVAL for any write whose length is
  not a whole `writesize` or whose offset is not write-size aligned.

So the first node a mkdir writes is refused with -EINVAL, and every mkdir returns it. The mount is
green because it only reads, which is why a read-only jffs2 looked healthy while every write was
dead.

Fix (`phase3l`): type the rootfs_data PARTITION as `MTD_NORFLASH` after the partition table is
registered, keeping `MTD_CAP_NANDFLASH` flags (so `MTD_BIT_WRITEABLE` stays clear and obsolete
marking stays off). That turns on jffs2's write buffer: nodes are accumulated and flushed as whole
write-size pages, which is exactly the shape this driver accepts. The master keeps MTD_NANDFLASH so
UBI on rootfsb and every other consumer see the real geometry. Verified in the linked image: the
store `mov r2, #3; strb r2, [r3]` sits immediately after the new `get_mtd_device_nm("rootfs_data")`
call in `luofu_fmc_probe` (c0327ca4).

## 2026-11-12 - PHASE B: C94 cannot carry a cross-boot latch; the persistence fire uses a build switch

The persistence proof needs one boot that leaves the jffs2 partition untouched (the seed test
otherwise erases it) and then checks the file the previous boot wrote. The obvious latch is C94:
the verdict survives the vendor fallback, so the seed test could skip the reseed when the previous
boot reported `0xC0DE9D0F`.

It cannot. The mach pet timer writes C94 every 5 s from the first second of a boot, and until the
mount test publishes a verdict it writes `0x9F0000xx`. The seed test is a `late_initcall`, long after
the first beat, so it always reads the pet's marker, never the previous boot's verdict.

The honest fix is a build switch, not another cell: `LUOFU_SEED_OFF` in `luofu_seed_test_init()`
compiles a build whose seed test does nothing and sets `luofu_preserve`, and in that build the mount
test *reads* `/mnt/new/persist.txt` and compares it with `LUFU-PERSIST\n` instead of writing it. The
file's presence and exact content after a reboot are then the primary evidence, and the write bit in
C94 is the secondary one.

## 2026-11-12 - PHASE B: the write buffer works; the ERASE MARKER is refused and every block goes bad

Fire `phase3l` (the partition typed MTD_NORFLASH) returned C94=0x9E801C1C: the partition is 8 MiB
(byte 0x80), and both mkdirs now return 0x1C = 28 = ENOSPC. The -EINVAL is gone, so jffs2's write
buffer is active and the node writes land. ENOSPC on a partition with 63 untouched blocks is the
next defect, and the source names it exactly.

`jffs2_mark_erased_block()` writes the erase-complete marker with `jffs2_flash_direct_writev()`, a
raw `mtd_write()` of `sizeof(struct jffs2_unknown_node)` = 12 bytes at the block's start. That is a
legal partial write on NOR, which is why the code is shaped that way, but this driver is a page
programmer: `luofu_mtd_write()` refuses any offset/length that is not a whole write-size unit with
-EINVAL. So every block jffs2 tried to erase failed at the marker write, `jffs2_erase_failed()`
moved it to the bad list, and the first mkdir found no space. The mount still succeeds because the
seed block is a valid partial-dirty block; only the erase path is dead.

`phase3o` routes that marker through `jffs2_flash_write()` (the write buffer) instead of the direct
write. Every other node already goes through it, the wbuf was flushed before the erase by
`jffs2_flush_wbuf_pad()`, and the flush is one whole write-size page, which is the shape this driver
accepts. The change is in `fs/jffs2/erase.c` and is a no-op for non-writebuffered devices because
`jffs2_flash_write()` falls back to the same direct write there.

Diagnosis chain, one fire per step: EINVAL (node write refused) -> write buffer -> ENOSPC (erase
marker refused) -> marker through the buffer.

## 2026-11-12 - PHASE C DESIGN: run the VENDOR init on our kernel, from the vendor squashfs root

The plan's Phase C is not "assemble the overlay in the kernel and pivot into it". The vendor already
knows how to do that: `/sbin/init` is procd, and the vendor's own preinit mounts `mtdblock15` at
`/mnt`, writes `upper/etc/mount_protect`, and `/sbin/mount_root` (fstools) builds the overlay from
the squashfs root and the jffs2 upper. Testing that chain is what the reversal needs, because it is
exactly the shape the final image has.

So the initramfs `/init` only has to get out of the way:
1. detach the kernel mount test's overlay and jffs2 mounts - jffs2 must NEVER be mounted twice, and
   the vendor's preinit mounts the same partition; two superblocks writing one flash corrupt it;
2. mount the vendor squashfs (`/dev/ubiblock0_0`, fallback `/dev/mtdblock13`) at `/newroot`;
3. move devtmpfs into the new root (the kernel mounted it on the initramfs /dev);
4. `pivot_root(".", ".")` + `umount2(".", MNT_DETACH)` (busybox switch_root's exact sequence);
5. `execve("/sbin/init")`.

The proof that the vendor userspace ran is a file, not a cell: the kernel mount test writes
`upper/etc/rc.local` on the jffs2 before the overlay exists, which shadows the squashfs rc.local
once mount_root builds the overlay, and `/etc/init.d/done` runs it at START=95. It writes
`/etc/procd-ran`, which lands in the jffs2 upper and is readable on the vendor afterwards.

Cells cannot carry this marker: by the time userspace runs, the pet timer owns C94 (it republishes
the mount verdict every 5 s), the log/home tick owns C18 and C1C, and the FMC read path owns C88 and
C98. The file is immune to all of them. The box also self-returns after 620 s (`LUOFU_HOME_TIMER_S`
-> `emergency_restart`), so the whole Phase C test is bounded without the watchdog.

## 2026-11-12 - PHASE B: phase3o hung inside the mount test; the erase path now needs a crumb ladder

Fire `phase3o` (cleanmarker through the write buffer) returned C94 = 0xC0DE9A01. That is not a mount
verdict at all: it is the mach's own `luofu_boot_stage` deposit (`late_initcall_sync`, written before
the mount test), and C18 = 0xC0DE52A1 is `luofu_restart` folding an UNCHANGED C04 (the UBI diag's
0xC0DE9A01) into its low byte. Both cells therefore say the same thing: the mount test never reached
its own C94 write.

The box did come back on its own at 14:41:45, and the link drop at 14:41:10 with C18 = 0xC0DE52A1
proves `luofu_restart` ran and its reset magic took. The home timer (`LUOFU_HOME_TIMER_S` = 620 s,
armed at the end of the FMC probe, ~14:30:50) is what returned it.

So `phase3o` is inconclusive about whether the marker write works: the boot hung somewhere inside the
mount test, after the jffs2 mount and before the verdict. The two candidates the source allows are
(a) the mkdir path now doing real erases, each erase verifying 128 KiB and writing a marker through
the write buffer, and (b) a deadlock in that new marker write.

`phase3s` therefore adds a crumb ladder to the mount test. Each step writes `0xC0DE9A00 | step` into
C04, which is exactly the value `luofu_restart` folds into C18's low byte, so a hang leaves
`C18 = 0xC0DE52E<n>` naming the last step entered:

    0xE1 entered            0xE2 jffs2 mounted
    0xE3 upper mkdir        0xE4 wk2 mkdir
    0xE5 overlay mounted    0xE6 write test returned

The Phase C rc.local shadow and the gmac/ethernet config are compiled out for this fire so the only
variable is the crumb ladder.

One hardening landed with it: `luofu_restart` now calls `del_timer_sync()` on the boot pet timer
before it parks. The boot pet keeps clearing the watchdog every 5 s, so a park with it alive is not
"the watchdog will do it" - it is a box that sits on this kernel until the pet's 600-beat budget runs
out. The reset magic took this time, so the box was not stranded, but the backstop was not a backstop.

## 2026-11-12 - PHASE B: the marker belongs in the DRIVER, not in jffs2's write buffer

The marker-through-wbuf change was wrong for a structural reason, not a tuning one. `__jffs2_flush_wbuf()`
assumes the caller owns `c->nextblock` (it dereferences `c->nextblock->allocated_refs`) and it
accounts the padded tail of the page against the block. The erase path calls the marker write while
`c->nextblock` is NULL - the source even comments "c->nextblock is NULL, no update to c->nextblock
allowed" at the flush-before-erase site - so routing a 12-byte marker through the wbuf from
`jffs2_mark_erased_block()` is not a supported shape. That is consistent with `phase3o`: the mount
test never published, which means it died inside the first mkdir that needed an erase.

The right layer is the driver. A NAND page is programmed as a whole page, and the MTD contract does
not say a write must be page-shaped, so the driver must do the merge:

    read the page (returns 0xff on a freshly erased page),
    overlay the caller's bytes,
    program the whole page.

The only partial write jffs2 issues is the erase-complete marker, and it always lands on a freshly
erased page, so the read-merge is exact. `luofu_mtd_write()` now takes that path for any write that
is not page-aligned and a whole number of pages; the page-aligned fast path is unchanged.

With this, `fs/jffs2/erase.c` goes back to upstream (`jffs2_flash_direct_writev`, 12 bytes) and the
patch recorded in the submodule is retired. `phase3t` is the fire.

## 2026-11-12 - PHASE C FIRE (phase3w) AND THE INJURY: the vendor came back with DNS only

`phase3w` ran the vendor-init path: our kernel's mount test assembled the overlay, `/init` detached the
lab mounts, mounted the vendor squashfs (`/dev/ubiblock0_0`, `/dev/mtdblock13` fallback), moved
devtmpfs, pivoted with `pivot_root(".", ".")` + `umount2(".", MNT_DETACH)`, and exec'd `/sbin/init`.

The box reset on schedule and is back at 192.168.10.1, but only port 53 answers. SSH (22), HTTP (80)
and HTTPS (443) are closed; ICMP and DNS answer, MAC 02:00:00:00:00:01 (documentation value; real MAC redacted). The fire script gave up at
poll 150: "VENDOR DID NOT RETURN".

The likely cause is cumulative: every seed-on fire erases the first 8 MiB of the vendor's own jffs2,
and this boot additionally let the vendor's preinit and `mount_root` run on that filesystem. The
vendor's `/etc/config` (dropbear, uhttpd) lives in the same partition, so those services no longer
start; dnsmasq still answers from built-ins. That is consistent with the vendor's own scan messages
and with the fact that the same box returned fully manageable after every Phase B fire.

Consequence for the plan: the seed-on strategy is not safe for Phase C. The lab must not leave the
vendor's config partition in a state the vendor's `mount_root` will reformat. Options for the next
attempt: keep the vendor's jffs2 untouched (no seed) and give our overlay a dedicated scratch
partition, or restore the vendor's config from the factory image before every vendor-init fire.

Recovery needs hands on the box: a power cycle first, then, if SSH/web do not return, a ~15 s RESET
hold for the TFTP door (`tftp/recovery.bin`, md5 421114c8ea999c925b7aa79cc548af81). After a successful
recovery the documented wizard + `passwd` + dropbear sequence restores manageable state.

## 2026-11-12 - PHASE C REWORK: the lab overlay moves off the vendor's config partition

The injury is structural, not a one-off: the lab's jffs2 upper and the seed test have been using
`rootfs_data`, which is the partition the vendor's own `/etc/config` (dropbear, uhttpd) lives on.
Every seed-on fire erased its first 8 MiB, and `phase3w` finally left the vendor with dnsmasq only.

The rework:
- the lab overlay upper, the seed test, the mount test's jffs2 mount and the NOR typing all move to
  the `upgrade` partition (mtd16, 29.5 MiB at 0x6280000). The vendor does not mount it at boot; its
  jffs2 scan of that partition is the "236 blocks" line that has always been in its dmesg, and it
  tolerates a valid filesystem there.
- `rootfs_data` is left to the vendor. The only write the lab makes to it is one targeted file:
  the initramfs `/init` mounts `/dev/mtdblock15`, writes `upper/etc/rc.local` (the proof marker),
  unmounts, and then pivots. A 100-byte file cannot take out a config partition the way an 8 MiB
  erase loop can.
- the mount test no longer writes the phase C shadow (`LUOFU_PHASE_C_SHADOW 0`); the shadow moved
  into `/init` where it belongs.

`phase3x` is the rebuilt slice: lab overlay on upgrade, vendor init from the squashfs, one targeted
rc.local write into rootfs_data. It cannot fire until the box is reachable again.

## 2026-11-12 - RECOVERY: the box came back with the first-run wizard, and the web session restored SSH

After `phase3w` the vendor answered only DNS. A power cycle did not help; the RESET hold brought the
box back with the Cudy FIRST-RUN WIZARD on port 80 (factory config: its `/etc/config` had been in the
partition the lab had erased). SSH was gone because dropbear's host keys were zero-byte files.

Restore sequence that worked (all over HTTP, no console):
1. GET `/cgi-bin/luci/` or `/cgi-bin/luci/admin/wizard`, take `_csrf` and `salt`.
2. The WIZARD takes ONE hash: POST `/cgi-bin/luci/admin/wizard` with
   `luci_password = sha256(pw + salt)` -> 302 and the admin password is set.
3. The LOGIN page that follows has an extra `token`: log in with
   `luci_password = sha256(sha256(pw + salt) + token)` -> 302 + `Set-Cookie: sysauth=...`.
4. With the session, POST `/cgi-bin/luci/admin/system/systime` with
   `timeclock` / `cbid.system.ntp.current` = `'; <command>; #` (the documented root command sink).
5. `echo PW > /tmp/.x; (cat /tmp/.x; cat /tmp/.x) | passwd root` sets the root password.
6. `rm -f /etc/dropbear/dropbear_*_host_key` and start dropbear directly:
   `dropbearkey -t ed25519 -f /etc/dropbear/dropbear_ed25519_host_key` then
   `/usr/sbin/dropbear -p 22 -R`; the project public key goes into `/etc/dropbear/authorized_keys`.
   The init script alone did nothing with zero-byte host keys; deleting them and starting the
   binary directly is what restored port 22. `/etc/init.d/dropbear enable` created S22dropbear.

After recovery: OpenWrt 22.03.6 / 2.4.15, 2 wiphys, 6 interfaces, calibration `[SUCC]` on both bands,
40 `hi_` modules, bootflag=a and boot_reg=0x10 (the vendor slot), ssh key login works.
The Phase C marker and `persist.txt` were destroyed with the old config partition, so `phase3w`'s
vendor-init run cannot be proven from the filesystem; the code path itself ran (the box reset on the
home timer and the vendor booted afterwards).

`phase3x` (vendor squashfs root + our /init, lab overlay on `upgrade`) booted, the mount test failed

vendor came back on ITS kernel (the /proc/mtd of the running box lists 17 partitions with no `lab`,
and C94 still holds 0x9ED80000, so the vendor never wrote it).

Two facts fell out of that run:
1. The lab scratch cannot be `upgrade`: 29.5 MiB is 236 eraseblocks, and the jffs2 mount has to scan
   all of it (minutes), on a partition the seed test can only prepare in a LATER boot. A dedicated
   8 MiB `lab` partition (the tail of the vendor's `upgrade` range, at 0x7780000) gives 64 blocks,
   which is the size every proven jffs2 test used.
2. The vendor's `rootfs_data` is 22 MiB (mtd15, 0x1600000); our DTS sees the first 8 MiB of it. Our
   /init mounts `/dev/mtdblock15` and drops the `upper/etc/rc.local` shadow there; the vendor's own
   mount sees the same start offset, so the shadow is visible to its mount_root.
3. The init is now INSTRUMENTED: every stage writes a tag into C94 through /dev/mem
   (0x6A01 vendor fs mounted, 0x6A02 + errno mount failed, 0x6A03 shadow written, 0x6A04 open
   failed, 0x6A05/0x6A06 squashfs source, 0x6A07 neither, 0x6A08 pivot done and execve attempted,
   0xF0xx a fail() exit). C94 survives a warm reset and the vendor never writes it, so the value
   read after the vendor returns names the exact stage. `fail()` writes 0xF0xx before it exits.

`phase3aa` = the instrumented init + the `lab` partition (seed/mount/typing retargeted), built
2026-11-12 16:25.

## 2026-11-12 - WHY NO CELL FROM THE INIT: /dev/mem write() returns EFAULT, mmap is the only working door

The initramfs init never left a crumb in C94 through `open("/dev/mem") + lseek() + write()`, and
that was the tooling, not the init. Measured on the vendor's own kernel with a freestanding ARM
test binary (source kept at /tmp/celltest.c during the session):

    open("/dev/mem", O_RDWR|O_SYNC)      -> fd 3
    lseek(fd, 0x10100C94, 0, SEEK_SET)   -> 0x10100c94  (SUCCESS)
    write(fd, &v, 4)                     -> 0xfffffff2 = -EFAULT
    mmap2(NULL, 4096, RW, SHARED, fd, 0x10100) -> 0xb6f16000, and p[0xC94/4] = v LANDS

So a file-position write through /dev/mem faults on this SoC (ARMv7, 5.10) while an mmap of the
same page writes fine. busybox `devmem` uses mmap for exactly this reason. `init-vendorroot.c` now
maps page 0x10100 once and stores the stage tag with a plain store. Two more traps fixed on the
way: the raw lseek ABI splits the 64-bit offset into r1:r2, and a mapped address like 0xb6f16000
is NEGATIVE as a signed long, so the mmap error check must compare against 0xfffff001, not 0.

Stage tags (also in the shadow rc.local, which writes 0xC0DE600D when the vendor's procd reaches
done): 0x6A00 init started, 0x6A01/0x6A02 vendor fs mounted/failed, 0x6A03/0x6A04 shadow
written/open failed, 0x6A05/0x6A06 squashfs source, 0x6A07 neither mount, 0x6A08 pivot done and
execve attempted, 0xF0xx fail() code. `phase3ae` carries the mmap cell writer and a 1500 s home
timer (was 620 s) so the vendor userspace has room to boot on our kernel.

## 2026-11-12 - Phase C instrumented: the init RUNS; mounts were never the problem, the pivot is

`phase3af` finally reported from inside the initramfs init: C94 = 0xC0DEF001, i.e. fail(1) after
BOTH squashfs mounts returned non-zero. Two tooling facts were established on the way, both by
running freestanding test binaries on the vendor's kernel:
- `/dev/mem` is not in devtmpfs (the mem driver registers a bare chrdev), so the init must mknod
  chr 1:1 itself; and a file-position write() to /dev/mem returns -EFAULT while an mmap of the same
  page plus a plain store works (busybox devmem uses mmap). The init now mmaps page 0x10100.
- mount()'s fifth argument is fine in r4 on this kernel (both the r4 and the stack-slot variants
  of a mount("tmpfs") test returned 0), so the mount ABI was never the bug.

`phase3ah` then pivoted into the squashfs the KERNEL MOUNT TEST already mounted at /mnt/lower
(a second mount of ubiblock0_0 while the first was lazily detached is what failed), and reported
C94 = 0xC0DEF003: fail(3), i.e. `pivot_root(".", ".")` was refused after chdir(/mnt/lower) worked.
`phase3ai` therefore records every errno in one accumulated word (0x6B000000 | tags: vendor-fs
mount errno bits 4-7, shadow-written bit 8, /dev-move errno 12-15, chdir errno 16-19, pivot_root
errno 20-23, chroot errno 24-27, exec bit 28) and falls back to chroot(".") when pivot_root is
refused, because the vendor's preinit only needs the squashfs as its root, not a namespace change.

One more recovery detail from the same session: after a factory reset dropbear refuses to start with
"Early exit: Bad buf_getptr" because the squashfs ships a ZERO-BYTE /etc/dropbear/dropbear_rsa_host_key
and dropbear parses it at startup. Removing the empty RSA/DSS key files and starting
`/usr/sbin/dropbear -p 22 -R` is what restores SSH; the ed25519 host key plus authorized_keys alone
are not enough while the empty file sits there.

## 2026-11-12 - phase3al: the stall is BEFORE the /dev move, and a shadow-free run leaves the config intact

`phase3al` removed the vendor-fs touch entirely (no mount, no shadow) and left only: tag, the two
lazy unmounts, the devtmpfs move, chdir(/mnt/lower), pivot_root or chroot, execve. C94 came back
0xD0FE6B01: low half 0x6B01 means the init ran and NOTHING after the first tag landed - not even the
/dev-move tag. So the stall in this build is in one of the calls between the first tag and the move:
the lazy `umount2("/overlay", MNT_DETACH)` (the mount test's jffs2 upper) or
`umount2("/mnt/new", MNT_DETACH)` (the overlay glue). A lazy unmount of a jffs2 whose write buffer
is dirty is a plausible synchronous flush point, which ties this stall to the same jffs2 write path
that stopped phase3ak's mkdir.

Useful counter-result: the box came back with its config INTACT (the LuCI login page, not the
wizard). Every earlier vendor-init attempt ended factory-default because OUR kernel had mounted the
vendor's config partition (and left a lazily detached, dirty superblock) before the vendor's own
mount_root saw it. A run that never touches rootfs_data does not trigger the vendor's rebuild.

C94 reporting caveat: the low 16 bits are ours and reliable, but the HIGH half read back is 0xD0FE,
not our 0xC0DE, in every post-init read. The vendor's kernel preserves a value written to C94 (a
0xC0DE1234 store read back exactly), so something on OUR kernel writes the upper half after the tag
store - most likely the driver's own crumb writes to C98 (0x9A000009 in the same reads). Treat only
the low half of a post-init C94 as the stage word until that is disentangled.

`phase3am` removes both lazy unmounts as well, so the only calls left before the pivot are mkdir
(EROFS on the read-only squashfs, harmless), the devtmpfs move, chdir, pivot/chroot and execve.

- Blocking: the first jffs2 WRITE/flush on our kernel stalls (phase3ak's mkdir under the upper,
  phase3al's stall before the /dev move with the lazy unmounts in between), and one build (phase3am)
  died in early boot. Until our kernel can complete a jffs2 write on the vendor's config partition,
  neither the rc.local shadow nor the vendor's own mount_root can finish on this kernel.
- Tooling caveat: only the LOW 16 bits of a post-init C94 are ours; the high half reads 0xD0FE.

The box ends this session on the vendor kernel, config intact (LuCI login page), ssh restored
(dropbear -p 22 -R after removing the squashfs's zero-byte RSA host key), 2 wiphys, 6 interfaces,
calibration SUCC on both bands, bootflag=a.

## 2026-11-12 20:31 - The stall is ABOVE the driver: no page program and no erase were ever attempted

`phase3an` carried crumbs inside luofu_fmc_write_page (C64: 0x77a0 entered / 0x77a1 completed /
0x77af failed, row in the low half) and luofu_fmc_erase_block (C68: 0x77e0/0x77e1/0x77ef). After the
run: C64 = 0 and C68 = 0. The init's vendor-fs mount succeeded (C94 low half 0x6B01) and then nothing
touched the driver at all - not one page program, not one block erase, and not even the mount test's
own write test (which writes through jffs2 and returned success, so its data stayed in the jffs2
write buffer and was never flushed).

So the stall is inside jffs2 above the mtd layer: block reservation, garbage collection, or the
write-buffer flush waiting on one of those. The most likely trigger is the TRUNCATED DEVICE: our DTS
gave rootfs_data 8 MiB of the vendor's 22 MiB partition, so jffs2 mounts a filesystem whose nodes and
free-space accounting were built for 0x1600000 bytes while it only sees 0x800000. With no free block
inside that window, every write and every mkdir waits for a GC pass that never finds one, and the GC
thread itself may be waiting on data outside the window.

`phase3ao` is the same image with rootfs_data at its real size (<0x4c80000 0x1600000>, which ends
exactly where `upgrade` starts at 0x6280000), so jffs2 sees the device the vendor's filesystem was
made for. The same crumbs stay in place: if the write now reaches the driver, C64 shows 0x77a1xxxx,
and if the shadow lands the tag gains bit 8.

## 2026-11-12 21:01 - PHASE C CLOSED: the vendor's own procd reached the end of boot on our kernel

`phase3ao` closed Phase C. Evidence, all read back from the vendor after the run:

    C94 = 0xC0DE600D                     (the value the shadow rc.local deposits)
    /overlay/upper/etc/procd-ran          -> "LUFU-PROCD"   (written by /etc/init.d/done)
    /overlay/upper/etc/rc.local           -> our 109-byte shadow script, still on the fs
    /proc/mtd on the running vendor       -> rootfs_data 0x1600000 (the vendor's own view)

The chain that ran: our initramfs init mounted `mtd:rootfs_data`, wrote the rc.local shadow into
`upper/etc`, moved devtmpfs into the squashfs, chrooted into the kernel-mounted vendor squashfs,
exec'd `/sbin/init`; the vendor's preinit and `mount_root` built the overlay on our kernel, procd
booted, and `/etc/init.d/done` executed our rc.local, which wrote procd-ran and deposited 0xC0DE600D
before starting dropbear. Every one of those steps is the vendor's own userspace, on our kernel.

ROOT CAUSE OF THE LONG STALL: the DTS gave `rootfs_data` 8 MiB of its real 22 MiB. jffs2 mounted a
filesystem built for 0x1600000 bytes inside an 0x800000 window, so its free-space accounting had no
allocatable block and every write or mkdir blocked in reservation/GC WITHOUT ever reaching the mtd
layer - which is exactly what the C64/C68 crumbs showed (no page program, no erase). Restoring the
real size (`<0x4c80000 0x1600000>`, ending where `upgrade` starts at 0x6280000) fixed the write path
and with it the whole vendor-init chain. The 8 MiB view was a lab artifact from when rootfs_data was
scratch; as a view of a 22 MiB filesystem it was silently self-defeating.

## 2026-11-13 05:37 - CORRECTION: the Phase C "closure" evidence is ambiguous, and the fix is a kernel-version check

The marker that closed Phase C cannot, by itself, prove WHICH kernel ran it. The initramfs init
writes `upper/etc/rc.local` into the vendor's config partition early; the vendor's own
`/etc/init.d/done` executes that file on EVERY boot of the box, including its own kernel. So
C94 = 0xC0DE600D plus `/etc/procd-ran` = LUFU-PROCD are produced equally well by
  (a) the vendor userspace running on OUR kernel, or
  (b) the stock vendor kernel booting later and running the same shadow rc.local.
`phase3ap`'s network dump exposed exactly this: it carries a full `ip addr`, `iw`, `lsmod` and dmesg
of the box, but its dmesg is the vendor's `Hi-GEMAC` driver and `uname -a` is `#0 SMP Sat Nov 25
18:18:57 2023`, i.e. the STOCK kernel ran that dump, not ours. The box had fallen back before our
kernel reached userspace.

So Phase C must be re-verified with a marker that names its kernel. `phase3aq` writes the rc.local
marker as:
  - append `"$(date +%s) $(uname -v)"` to `/kernel-ran.log` (a log, not a rewrite, so every boot
    that runs the shadow leaves a line);
  - append the same kernel version plus the full network dump to `/net-state.log`;
  - deposit `0xC0DE600E` when `uname -v` matches `*2023*` (the stock kernel) and `0xC0DE600D`
    otherwise.
After a run, a line in `/kernel-ran.log` carrying the 2026 build string is the proof that OUR kernel
reached the vendor userspace's `done`; a log with only the 2023 line means it did not, and the
C94 value is a leftover from the stock boot. Until that line is read, Phase C is CANDIDATE, not
closed.

## 2026-11-13 12:18 - The reset is BELOW the kernel: the panic notifier never ran

`phase3bb` put a fixed magic (0xdead0a17) at the very end of the FMC driver's panic notifier, in C98,
a cell that has preserved this driver's crumbs across every vendor fallback. After the crash, C98
read 0x9A000009 - the driver's last ordinary read crumb - not the magic. So:

    the kernel never panicked; the box resets below panic().

That closes the capture question from the other direction: no pstore record was expected, because no
panic dump ever runs. The panics found in mtd10 before the erase were the stock kernel's own
(hi_* modules), never ours.

What resets the SoC below the kernel: the vendor's hardware watchdog is the leading suspect. The
mach-luofu code arms a "watchdog pet timer, 5 s period" (visible in our kernel's dmesg as
`luofu: watchdog pet timer armed, 5 s period`), and the standalone luofu-wdt driver was lost with the
gmac/mdio sources. If the pet timer stops, or its register write does nothing, the armed WDT fires on
its own timeout and the box is back on the vendor with no panic to show. That also explains the
run-to-run variance: #162 and a couple of later boots lived the full 25 minutes, while most die
within seconds - a pet that works only sometimes.

Cheap discriminator, next fire: have the initramfs init sleep ~6 s and read C94 twice. The pet writes
a beat every 5 s, so two different values mean the pet is alive and the WDT is being fed; two
identical values mean the kernel is not petting and the WDT reset theory is confirmed. That is one
initramfs change, no driver work, and it settles the last remaining explanation for a reset that
leaves no kernel trace.

## 2026-11-13 14:02 - #170: the disarm did not save it; the vendor's own driver names the watchdog

`phase3bc` (LAB BUILD disarming the hsan watchdog at boot with the vendor's stop magic) produced:

    S10boot 1763001082  #170 SMP Fri Nov 13 13:34:43 +07 2026   (ours)
    S95done 1763001114                                          (ours, done ran)
    S10boot 1763001118  #0 SMP Sat Nov 25 18:18:57 2023         (vendor, 4 s later)

So even with the stop magic written to CRG+0x64 the box still resets about four seconds after our
S95done, and the marker inside done never got its writes to flash. Either the stop magic is not the
right disarm for this watchdog, or the reset is not the watchdog at all.

The vendor's own kernel names the device and its parameters:

    hsan-watchdog-driver 14880000.watchdog: Hsan watchdog timeout=30 sec, nowayout=1
    /dev/watchdog and /dev/watchdog0 exist

So the watchdog lives in the SAME 0x14880000 page the mach code pets (CRG+0x70 clear, +0x64 enable are
the vendor DT's clr/en offsets), it times out in 30 s, and nowayout=1 means nothing ever stops it. The
~30 s timing fits every early reset in this session, including #170's death 4 s after done (done lands
around 30 s after boot). That makes the pet shim the prime suspect even after the disarm attempt: if
the shim's 5 s period is not real in wall-clock terms (its own comments record a measured ~1.74 s per
beat and a 600-beat budget), the clear can arrive too late, and if the disarm magic is not what this
driver expects, the stop write is a no-op.

The clean fix is not another magic: it is the luofu-wdt driver that was lost with the gmac/mdio
sources. Its probe sets WDOG_HW_RUNNING and the watchdog core pings it through the standard path, with
a real 30 s margin, instead of a mach shim guessing at register semantics. Until that driver exists,
every long run is a race against a 30 s timer.

## 2026-11-13 14:36 - A userspace keeper in the init (phase3bf)

The fix that does not depend on either mechanism: the initramfs init now forks a child right before
exec'ing the vendor's init. That child creates /dev/watchdog (misc 10:130), opens it, and writes the
keepalive byte every 5 s forever. Because the driver is in the image, the open binds to the real
luofu-wdt, whose ping is the vendor's own clear sequence, so the timer is fed by the same path the
vendor's procd would use - but from the first second and independent of procd's schedule.

The init binary (4356 B) was embedded and verified in the built image (usr/initramfs_inc_data
decompresses to the new /init, which contains the /dev/watchdog string). phase3bf is the slice under
test.

      1763001399 #0  SMP Sat Nov 25 18:18:57 2023 shadow         <- vendor, 38 s later

be turned off without restructuring the platform config; the lab fix is to emit the same
tag from arch/arm/include/asm/vermagic.h while keeping the patching. Our kernel's vermagic
now reads "5.10.201 SMP mod_unload ARMv7", character-for-character what the vendor's

  hi_kmac/hi_swa modules loading instead, ours can stay as it is.

phase3bi is the vermagic-matched build under test.

## 2026-11-13 22:13 - The keeper race: a failed open left the armed watchdog unfed

then sleeps and writes to nothing while U-Boot's 30 s timer runs out. The open now retries every beat,
so a late-registering driver is picked up instead of being missed forever.

## 2026-11-14 00:40 - The vendor MDIO read, disassembled: our poll polarity was inverted

The vendor's hi_kmdio.ko (/lib/hisilicon/ko/hi_kmdio.ko, pulled as gzip-hex over ssh) carries the
symbols hi_mdio_read and hi_mdio_write. Disassembling hi_mdio_read with the lab toolchain shows the
real handshake, and our driver got two things backwards:

    0x314  mov r2,#13 ; str r2,[ip]          command 0x0d goes to +0x00 FIRST
    0x338  ldr r2,[r1] ; ands r2,r2,#15      read-status at +0x6c
    0x340  bne 0x330                         NON-ZERO -> keep looping (busy)
    0x344..0x378                             frame assembled, written to +0x70 only AFTER the status clears
    0x394  ldr r2,[lr] ; ands #15 ; beq      write-status at +0x60: ZERO -> keep looping (waits for NON-zero)
    0x3a0  str r2,[ip,#96]                   acknowledge by writing the status value back
    0x3d4  str r2,[ip,#112]                  the frame written a second time
    0x3ec  poll +0x60 until NON-zero, acknowledge again
    0x3fc  ldr r0,[ip,#116] ; uxth r0,r0     data read from +0x74, low 16 bits

Our body wrote the frame first, then the command, then polled the read-status waiting for NON-zero
(the inverse of the vendor's done condition) and gave up. Every transfer timed out for that reason.

phase3cd implements the vendor's sequence: command, wait for the read-status low nibble to read ZERO,
write the frame, wait for the write-status low nibble to become NON-ZERO, acknowledge it, write the
frame again, acknowledge again, read the data. The frame encoding is still ours; if the PHYs answer
but with wrong register values, that encoding is the next comparison against the vendor's bit tricks
at 0x344-0x378.

## 2026-11-14 01:08 - The handshake order was necessary but not sufficient; the frame word is next

phase3cd ran the vendor's four-phase handshake (command, wait-for-zero, frame, wait-for-nonzero, ack,
frame, ack, data) and the controller still times out with the data line at 0xff92. The remaining
difference is the frame word itself. Our luofu_mdio_frame() builds (phy << 8) | reg; the vendor builds
it at hi_mdio_read+0xcc..0x100 with a bit pattern we do not reproduce:

    0x344  and r6, r6, #31          phy & 31
    0x34c  bfi r1, r2, #16, #16     high half seeded from the status value
    0x354  mvn r2, r6, lsl #17
    0x358  and r4, r4, #31          reg & 31
    0x360  movw r0, #0x60e0
    0x364  mvn r2, r2, lsr #17      the rotate trick that places the opcode/start bits
    0x368  and r0, r0, r1, lsr #16
    0x36c  orr r2, r2, r4, lsl #8
    0x370  orr r2, r2, r0
    0x374  bfi r1, r2, #16, #16
    0x378  str r1, [ip, #112]       the frame word

so the high half carries (start | opcode | phy) in a layout the controller expects, and the `mvn/lsr`
pair is the standard rotate-immediate the compiler emits for a constant mask. Decoding those two
instructions exactly is the next step, then replacing luofu_mdio_frame() with the decoded layout.

Everything else stands: criterion 1 PASS (named stop step), criterion 3 PASS (wireless line builds),
criterion 4 PASS (tree clean, ledger current). Criterion 2 remains open on this one frame word.

## 2026-11-14 01:56 - The vendor frame decoded: 0x8000 | (reg << 8) | phy

Emulating hi_mdio_read's frame assembly (0x344..0x378) for every address pair gives a clean layout:

    phy=2  reg=1  -> 0x8102
    phy=4  reg=1  -> 0x8104
    phy=2  reg=4  -> 0x8402
    phy=0  reg=0  -> 0x8000
    phy=31 reg=31 -> 0x9f1f

i.e. frame = 0x8000 | (reg << 8) | phy - the start bit in bit 15, the register in bits 12..8, the PHY
address in bits 4..0. Our luofu_mdio_frame() built (phy << 8) | reg: the two fields SWAPPED and no
start bit. That is why the controller never began a transaction regardless of the handshake order: we
were addressing the wrong register on a (mostly) nonexistent PHY with a frame that had no start pulse.

phase3ce carries the corrected layout with the vendor's four-phase handshake.

## 2026-11-14 02:56 - The two frame words differ: the second is the command phase

Decoding the second assembly at hi_mdio_read+0x3ac..0x3d4 gives a second word distinct from the first:

    phy=2  reg=1  -> first 0x8102, second 0xc102
    phy=4  reg=1  -> first 0x8104, second 0xc104
    phy=2  reg=4  -> first 0x8402, second 0xc402
    phy=0  reg=0  -> first 0x8000, second 0xc000
    phy=31 reg=31 -> first 0x9f1f, second 0xdf1f

so the second word is the first with bit 14 set (0xc000 | reg << 8 | phy). Our driver wrote the SAME
word twice. phase3cf writes 0x8000|... for the address phase and 0xc000|... for the command phase,
each followed by the write-status wait and acknowledgement, then reads +0x74.

## 2026-11-14 03:23 - Two-phase frames still time out; the vendor passes a FLAGS-encoded command

phase3cf wrote both decoded words (0x8000|reg<<8|phy, then the same with bit 14) with the vendor's
handshake and the same result: every transfer times out and luofu_mdio_read returns -110, which the
diagnostic cell shows as 0xff92.

Re-reading hi_mdio_read's entry exposes what is still missing: it treats its THIRD argument as a flags
word, not a register number -

    0x2c0  ands r2, r4, #0x40000000     bit 30: the read path (writes cmd 0x0d to +0x00)
    0x2cc  ands r4, r4, #0x20000000     bit 29: a second path (writes the flags to +0x00, waits on +0x60)
    0x2d4  str  r4, [ip]                neither bit: writes 0 to +0x00 and tails into another routine

So the vendor's mii read is not called with (phy, reg); it is called with an encoded command whose high
bits select the operation and whose low bits carry the register. Our driver writes a bare 0x0d to +0x00
and assumes the frame carries everything, which is not how this controller is driven. Decoding that
encoding from the callers (hi_mdio_probe installs the mii_bus ops; the phy driver calls back through
them) is the next step, and it is the last unexplained difference between our driver and the vendor's.

Everything is committed; criteria 1, 3 and 4 PASS, criterion 2 open on this command encoding.

## 2026-11-14 03:57 - The register map came from a DEAD code path; the real one is 0x20/0x2c/0x30/0x38

The probe stores hi_mdio_read as the mii_bus read op (MOVW/MOVT at 0x98..0xa0), so that function is
reachable - but only through the flag paths. For a plain register number (0-31) both flags tested at
its entry (bit 30, bit 29) are zero, so it takes the tail call at 0x2d4 into the routine at 0x17c, and
THAT routine uses a different register set:

    0x17c  ip = 0x5F5E100 (bounded count)
    0x1a4  ldr r3,[base+0x2c] ; ubfx r3,#16,#3 ; loop while non-zero     wait for bits 18:16 to clear
    0x1b4  frame = (~(phy<<17))>>17 inverse | ((reg<<8) & 0x1f00)        the 0x8000|reg|phy word
    0x1e0  str frame,[base+0x30]                                        the frame register is 0x30
    0x1fc  ldr r3,[base+0x20] ; (v | v>>1) & 1 ; loop while zero        wait for bit0/bit1
    0x20c  str v,[base+0x20]                                            acknowledge
    0x224  ldr r2,[base+0x2c] ; tst #0x70000 ; loop while set           wait for the status to clear
    0x230  ldr r0,[base+0x38] ; uxth                                    data lives at 0x38

So every offset this driver was built on (0x00 command, 0x60 write-status, 0x6c read-status, 0x70
frame, 0x74 data) belongs to the extended/DFX path and matches nothing the bus op actually touches.
That is why the clock, the frame layout and the handshake order all had to be right and the controller
still never answered: it was being driven through registers it never reads.

phase3cg implements the real sequence on 0x2c/0x30/0x20/0x38 with the decoded frame and bounded waits.

## 2026-11-14 04:24 - All four MDIO hypotheses tested; the remaining suspect is the switch in front of it

Six builds have now exercised every element the vendor module exposes: the clock (real, 100 MHz), the
handshake order, the frame layout (0x8000|reg<<8|phy plus the bit-14 command word) and the register map
the bus op actually reaches (0x20 acknowledge, 0x2c status bits 18:16, 0x30 frame, 0x38 data). Every
one of them times out, and the diagnostic cell shows -110 truncated to 0xff92.

What that eliminates is as useful as what it proves. It is not the gate, not the frame, not the poll
order and not the offsets - with those all correct the controller still never raises a completion bit.
The remaining difference from the vendor's boot is the stack in front of it: the vendor loads hi_swa,

therefore hi_kmdio) sitting on top of that switch bring-up. On our kernel the lsw nodes only get their
gate clocks enabled and their resets released by the gmac driver's switch branch (diag 6201/6202);
nothing programs the internal LSW. The MDIO's five PHYs hang off that switch, so no completion bit may
ever arrive until the switch is brought up.

Next steps, in order: (1) read the vendor's hi_swa/hi_lsw_dp init sequence and find the minimum register
programming that makes the switch pass MDIO through - the modinfo deps and the dmesg ordering both say
it runs first; (2) if that is a large port, test the alternative directly: bit-bang MDIO over the two
pins the vendor's pinctrl shows for the mdio node, which bypasses the controller entirely.

State: criteria 1, 3, 4 PASS (committed). Criterion 2 open, now attributed to the internal switch rather
than to the MDIO controller. The box is healthy on the vendor kernel.

## 2026-11-14 12:22 - Why the vendor's modules could not load: our kernel placed them FAR

arch/arm/kernel/module.c's module_alloc tries the near window (MODULES_VADDR..MODULES_END) first and,
with CONFIG_ARM_MODULE_PLTS=y, falls back to the far vmalloc region whenever that fails - PLTs then
bridge the distance. The vendor's modules were built against a kernel that never needed PLTs, so their
ELF has no .plt sections, and once a load is placed far every relocation over 32 MB dies with exactly
the message we kept seeing: "module PLT section(s) missing".

So the vermagic work was necessary but the placement was the actual wall. phase3ch removes the far
fallback (a load that cannot fit near now fails honestly) and prints the allocation address and size:

    luofu: module_alloc <size> bytes -> <addr> (near region only)

If the vendor's hi_* stack then loads, its own switch/MDIO/MAC drivers run on our kernel and the
Ethernet milestone stops depending on any of our re-derived register maps.

## 2026-11-14 14:27 - The module loader refused every module that had no .plt, before checking whether one was needed

module_frob_arch_sections() (arch/arm/kernel/module-plts.c) fails the load the moment a module carries

of their ELF files has those sections - and neither did any module fail for a real range problem. The
check fires before any relocation is examined, which is why every module on our kernel failed, the
kernel's own crypto helpers included, and why lsmod was empty.

phase3cj makes the sections optional in two places:
- module_frob_arch_sections: a module without .plt logs one line and continues;
- get_module_plt: if a relocation ever genuinely needs a PLT and the module has none, it prints the
  target and location and returns the value unchanged, so the existing range check fails the load
  honestly with the distance written down instead of dereferencing a null section.

is the vendor's own situation. If this works, the vendor's hi_* stack loads and its switch, MDIO, MAC
and PHY drivers run on our kernel - the whole Ethernet milestone with no further reverse engineering.

## 2026-11-14 22:13 - EINVAL explained: the ARM finit_module number is 379, not 350

The diagnostic log named it exactly. Every patched module opened fine and every load returned -22
(EINVAL):

    hi_basic fd=0 ret=-22
    hi_kmdio fd=0 ret=-22
    hi_swa   fd=0 ret=-22
    (22 lines, all -22; hi_kteam fd=-2, no such file - it is built per-board)

EINVAL before module_alloc, with the file found and the vermagic matching, is the syscall contract
check at the top of finit_module: flags outside MODULE_INIT_IGNORE_MODVERSIONS|IGNORE_VERMAGIC return
-EINVAL. The init was calling 350, which is the x86_64 number. The ARM table in
arch/arm/tools/syscall.tbl says:

    379  common  finit_module  sys_finit_module

So our init was invoking an unrelated ARM syscall with (fd, "", 0) and getting EINVAL from it. This is
the second x86-ism to bite the freestanding init; the mount/open/write numbers happened to match, which
is why only this call failed. Fixed to 379 and refired.

## 2026-11-14 23:5x - The MDIO controller protocol, decoded from the live driver

The vendor's hi_kmdio.ko was never a bit-bang. Its bus op reaches a helper at 0x17c (read) and 0xa4
(write) which drive an MMIO controller with FOUR registers, not the 0x60/0x70/0x74 set the driver had
been using (those belong to the DFX/extended path):

    base+0x2c  status, bits 18:16 non-zero = busy
    base+0x30  the frame word
    base+0x20  write-status: bit0|bit1 set = complete, write the value back to acknowledge
    base+0x38  read data, low 16 bits

and the frame itself is assembled in the HIGH half:

    read : ((0x8000 | reg<<8 | phy) << 16)          written to base+0x30
    write: ((0x8000 | reg<<8 | phy) << 16) | data   written to base+0x30

The sequence: wait 0x2c[18:16]==0, write the frame, poll 0x20 bit0|bit1, acknowledge, wait 0x2c[18:16]==0,
read 0x38. The driver was writing the frame UNSHIFTED, which is why the controller never started a
transaction no matter how the handshake was ordered. Fixed; the sequence now matches the vendor's
instruction-for-instruction.

## The Genius PHY, identified locally

hi_kphy.ko's .data holds its phy_driver match at +0x50: phy_id 0x20669a00, mask 0xffffff00. The module
also loads a patch file (lsw/hi_ephy_%xv%x.bin) into the PHY - that download is the one piece of the
vendor PHY we do not reproduce yet, and the new driver documents it as the known gap rather than
pretending it is done.

drivers/net/ethernet/luofu/luofu-phy.c now registers that ID with the genphy operations. Together with
luofu-mdio and luofu-gmac the kernel has a complete clean-room network chain: MDIO controller, Genius
PHY and GEMAC. All three build into the image.

The dmesg line to look for is `Hi-GEMAC ... eth2: PHY [14000000.mdio0:04] driver [Luofu Genius PHY]`.
If it appears, M2's core is proven with our code alone on the network path.

  - our MDIO completes real C22 transfers - the phy_id reads back 0x20669a09, which is the vendor's
    0x20669a00 plus revision 9, the byte the 0xffffff00 mask ignores. The register decode and the
    high-half frame are correct, proven on hardware;
  - our GEMAC attaches all four ports through phylink and trains eth2 to gigabit;
  - the bus is ours: every PHY device is a child of 14000000.mdio0.

The PHY driver that bound is the vendor's hi_kphy, because the init loads it at ~2 s while the platform
devices probe at ~29 s, so it is first in the match list. That is the one remaining vendor network
module, and dropping it from the init list is the next boot: our built-in luofu-phy (phy_id 0x20669a00,
mask 0xffffff00, genphy ops) then binds instead and the network chain becomes fully clean-room except
for the LSW switch, which is M3.

## 2026-11-15 01:30 - The no-op shadow was a mistake: hi_kpinctrl is load-bearing

phase3db replaced /etc/rc.d/luofu with `exit 0` to stop the vendor's PHY driver from winning the match.
The box never came back: 150 polls, no vendor return, SSH closed.

Reading the script from rootfs-2.5.24 shows why. Its FIRST action is

    insmod /lib/hisilicon/ko/hi_kpinctrl.ko

and our init's own attempt to load that module fails with -ENOENT on an unresolved symbol. Without the
pinctrl, the MDIO and Ethernet pins are never muxed, no PHY is visible on the bus, eth2 never comes up,
and the box is unreachable. The script also sets the CPU governor, the PIE IRQ affinity, ip_forward,
conntrack limits and the temperature sensors - all of which the stock boot expects.

The box is in the watchdog loop: our image boots, the network does not come up, the keeper's home timer
resets it, the bootflag still points at our image. Recovery is the U-Boot boot count fallback after
enough attempts, or a power cycle to add attempts faster. A monitor is armed on the SSH port.

The fix, built and waiting: the shadow now runs the vendor's own script with ONLY the three modules our
drivers own filtered out:

    sed -e '/hi_kphy\.ko/d' -e '/hi_kmdio\.ko/d' -e '/hi_kmac\.ko/d' /rom/etc/rc.d/luofu

so pinmux, IRQ affinity, sysctls and everything else stay intact, and our luofu-phy finally gets the
match. Lesson recorded: on this board, any overlay shadow of a vendor script must be a filtered copy of
the original, never a replacement.

## 2026-11-15 04:10 - The init's /vendor mount is read-only on this strap

The instrumented boot produced no `luofu-init: wfile` lines at all, and that is itself the answer: the
init cannot write to /dev/kmsg either, so the logging path is gone with the write path. The evidence:

    /overlay/upper/         etc/ (stock), lib/ (written 05:48 by the lab stage), sbin/
                            -> no boot.log, no mod-load.log, no net-dump-final.txt
    /overlay/upper/etc/rc.d -> only K50dropbear/S22dropbear from the stock
    the init's vmods load prove /vendor is READABLE (all modules resident)

(/vendor), and earlier boots DID write through it (phase3cv's mod-load.log exists, dated 21:45), so this
is strap-dependent, not a code regression: the init mounts /dev/mtdblock15 with fstype jffs2 and flags
0. On this board the block device comes up read-only in some strap states (mtdblock opens read-only
unless something has opened the MTD for writing first), which exactly matches "works sometimes".

The fix is in the init's mount: mount jffs2 with the "rw" data option and check the result, and if that
still yields a read-only superblock, remount rw before writing. The mount's errno is already tagged into
C18, so one more fire names it even if the writes stay silent.

Until then the system is safe but the lab boot runs the vendor's script in full (hence the vendor PHY
winning the match): the network, the web and the broker channel all work, so the box is recoverable and
VERIFIABLE at every point - only the M2 ownership of the PHY is pending.

## 2026-11-15 18:45 - 3df debugged off the box: the wfile channel works, and it is the kmsg line nobody read

The bench cannot give us a console (UART RX dead), so the 3df init was run under QEMU
instead. Setup: `qemu-system-arm` 11.1.3, machine `virt`, cortex-a15; a kernel built from
this tree in a separate copy (`build/linux-kbuild/qemu-src`, so the device tree is
untouched) with `ARCH_LUOFU`, `ARCH_VEXPRESS` and `CONFIG_MTD_UBI` enabled; the tracked
`init-vendorroot.c` compiled static and passed as `rdinit`.

Result, in order: the kernel boots to userspace and prints our banner on a PL011 console;
the FMC's own hooks run (`seed test wret=-1`, `overlay test j1=-19`); and the 3df init
prints all seven `wfile()` calls, in source order:

    /vendor/upper/etc/rc.d/S10boot E=2
    ... all seven ... /vendor/upper/pstore-check.txt E=2

so the instrument's kmsg channel works and was live. Every earlier fire judged silence
from the C98 cell or from the pstore/RAM log ring, and the ring is scrubbed by the stock
boot; the kmsg lines are the one readout that reaches `dmesg` whenever the boot reaches
userspace. The `E=2` values themselves are a property of the emulated run (no
`/dev/mtdblock0`, so the init's mount never happened) and are not a board measurement.

Two build facts fell out that were not obvious:

- `drivers/mtd/nand/luofu/luofu-fmc.c` does not compile without `CONFIG_MTD_UBI`
  (`luofu_phase_cell`, `luofu_log_b` sit inside `#ifdef CONFIG_MTD_UBI` regions), and
  `MTD_PSTORE` pulls `PSTORE`/`PSTORE_BLK` in. A config fragment missing any of those
  fails to link or fails to compile. The device config happens to carry them.
- `scripts/gcc-plugins` breaks when `DEBUG_LL` is enabled; the QEMU build disables
  `CONFIG_GCC_PLUGINS` rather than debug the plugin.

The emulator is not luofu silicon: no FMC, no `sysenv`, no bus timing. What it does give
is a full console for every path the init and the FMC's init hooks own, for free, with no
TFTP recovery. Evidence and the reproduce line:
`build/linux-kbuild/waves/3df/emulation.md` (a copy also sits in `qemu-src/`).

Next bench action, when the box is fired again: read the `wfile()` verdict from
`dmesg | grep /vendor/upper`, not from C98 and not from pstore. It decides EROFS vs
ENOENT in one read and costs no extra flash cycle.

## 2026-11-15 19:05 - Emulation closes the init-side question: the shadow writes work when /vendor mounts

The 3df init was taken as far as an emulator can take it. With a real jffs2 image stapled
into guest RAM (`-device loader,file=...,addr=0x5c000000`) and exposed as `mtd:rootfs_data`
(`mem=448M phram.phram=rootfs_data,0x5c000000,0x2000000`), the tracked init mounts it and
all seven `wfile()` calls land:

    /vendor/upper/etc/rc.d/S10boot OK
    /vendor/upper/etc/init.d/luofu OK
    /vendor/upper/etc/rc.d/luofu OK
    /vendor/upper/etc/rc.d/S18hyfibrd OK
    /vendor/upper/etc/rc.d/S20network OK
    /vendor/upper/etc/rc.d/S95done OK
    /vendor/upper/pstore-check.txt OK

Without a jffs2 image the same run says `E=2` on every line. So on the console the verdict
word separates three states: `OK` (write landed), `E=2` (path absent: the mount did not
produce `/vendor/upper/etc/rc.d`), anything else (a different errno). The init, its mount,
its append and its verdict line are all correct software; nothing in them needs fixing
before the next fire.

Four build facts learned, all cheap to repeat and expensive to rediscover:
- `CONFIG_JFFS2_FS` is not in `hisi_defconfig`; without it every jffs2 mount is `E=2`.
- `luofu-fmc.c` needs `CONFIG_MTD_UBI`, `MTD_PSTORE` needs `PSTORE`+`PSTORE_BLK`, and
  `init/main.c` calls `luofu_overlay_verdict`, so `ARCH_LUOFU` cannot be disabled.
- `phram` maps zeroed guest RAM: load the image with `-device loader` or the mount sees
  no valid jffs2 nodes (`E=5`).
- A `qemu-src` tree that was both reconfigured and rebuilt stopped reaching userspace on
  `virt` (SIGILL for a known-good init) while a fresh `qemu-baseline` copy with the same
  options ran everything. Keep the fiddled tree and the baseline tree separate.

What emulation cannot say: the phram is SRAM-backed MTD, not the FMC; NAND geometry, ECC
and timing are absent, and the mount takes 8.6 s where the live FMC is far quicker. The
overlay test still reports `j1=-2`/`-19` because this host has no `rootfsb` or `lab`
partition. That is the boundary; anything past it is the board's.

Evidence: `build/linux-kbuild/waves/3df/emulation.md` (reproduce block included),
`/tmp/realm-3df.log`, and the baseline kernel at `build/linux-kbuild/qemu-baseline`.

landed write from a missing path from a real error. (2) The audit's "prerequisite hunk 0"
premise is wrong on this kernel: `mkdir("/dev")` returns `-EEXIST` even though the cpio has
only `./init`, and the `devtmpfs` mount right after it returns 0. (3) The init's
`/vendor` mount is a direct `SYS_mount`, not a `mount(8)` call, and the kernel matched
the zero-length fstype by name, so a missing userspace binary is not the failure mode.

So: the init is correct software. If the next 3df boot reaches userspace and prints
`E=2`, the `/vendor` mount failed to produce `/vendor/upper/etc/rc.d` on luofu's FMC; if it
prints `OK`, the shadow landed and the remaining question is the vendor `hi_kphy` binding.
If the boot never reaches userspace at all, the emulator still cannot help: that path is
kernel or hardware.

Emulation's boundary, stated plainly: phram is SRAM-backed MTD, not the FMC; no NAND
geometry, ECC or timing is exercised; mount here takes 8.6 s where the live FMC is far
quicker; the FMC's own hooks report `j1=-2`/`-19` only because this host has no `rootfsb`
or `lab` partition. Both non-fatal probes are expected in emulation.

Four build facts, cheap to repeat and expensive to rediscover: `CONFIG_JFFS2_FS` is not in
`hisi_defconfig` (every jffs2 mount is then `E=2`); `luofu-fmc.c` needs `CONFIG_MTD_UBI`,
`MTD_PSTORE` needs `PSTORE`+`PSTORE_BLK`, and `ARCH_LUOFU` cannot be disabled because
`init/main.c` calls `luofu_overlay_verdict`; `phram` maps zeroed RAM, so the image must go
in with `-device loader` or jffs2 sees `E=5`; and a reconfigured `qemu-src` tree stopped
reaching userspace on `virt` (SIGILL for a known-good init) while a fresh
`qemu-baseline` copy with the same options ran everything.

Evidence and the reproduce block: `build/linux-kbuild/waves/3df/emulation.md`. Logs:
`/tmp/realm-3df.log` (all `OK`), `/tmp/mkdirtest.log` (`EEXIST` + mount 0). Commit
`39d8732` carries the first version of this finding.

## 2026-11-16 17:35 - The bench lost its only write path: the vendor loader cannot boot our slot A and cannot be prompted

The reset hold did not buy a recovery, it exposed the floor. The capture
`build/uart-logs/20261116T103014Z-recover-3dk.log` holds the cycle: U-Boot tries A
(`bootflag a bootreg 11`), the FIP fallback prints the image header and dies with a `data abort`
inside U-Boot (`r5=0x834d3bae`), it falls to B (`bootflag b bootreg 10`), the stock 4.1 MB kernel
starts, reaches `Run /init`, and panics at 10.8 s on the ShuangTa PCIe quirk in `jffs2_gcd_mtd15`.
The watchdog resets it into the next pass. The fault is not size: 3dg's 2.78 MB kernel reached the
same four header lines and aborted the same way, and 3dh's 2.96 MB kernel booted whenever it was
reached by the countdown path, which prints `alias console=...` and `Uncompressing Linux...`.
The countdown path is only reached when `bootreg` is 0 (POR sets `bootreg init, set 10`; the 05:23
recovery capture shows `bootreg 0` on that boot); the fallback path is entered whenever a slot is
flagged failed, and it corrupts the flags on its way through.

Two options were checked and closed. The serial prompt is unreachable: the 2026-11-08 floods with
and without `bootstopkey` both booted Linux, and `HARDWARE-IDENTITY.md` records that the router-side
RX pad never receives. A manual slot-A load from a network boot is also closed: `bootfip` is
`bootcmd` and the vendor env writes both slots with one image
(`fipupdate_eth=...mtd erase kernela;mtd write kernela...;mtd erase kernelb;mtd write kernelb...`
in `dumps/router-20261108/enva.bin`), so this loader accepts only a FIP package even when it is
handed one.

So the bench step is the vendor recovery: RESET held through power-on, `recovery.bin` over TFTP from
192.168.1.88, which is Cudy's own WR3000 v2 procedure
(https://www.cudy.com/en-gb/blogs/faq/how-to-recovery-the-cudy-router-from-openwrt-firmware-to-cudy-official-firmware).
The host lane passes a self-test: the server on UDP 69 answered a local RRQ for `recovery.bin`
(`421114c8ea999c925b7aa79cc548af81`, 20,975,775 bytes), `enp195s0f3u1` carries `192.168.1.88/24`,
and ufw allows `69/udp on enp195s0f3u1`. The stock-slot filesystem is also degraded (JFFS2 refuses
to erase blocks, the read-only squashfs returns ECC errors), so the recovery is wanted for its own
sake, not only as an unlock.

Left armed: the console capture (`timeout 600`) and the TFTP server; their PIDs and logs are in
`/tmp/arm-3dk.env` and `/tmp/arm-3dk-tftp.env`.

The durable rule for the next session: a slice can only be written while a booting userspace
exists, and a slice that does not boot costs a Cudy recovery, so every fire needs a recovery plan
before it is started. Procedure: `build/linux-kbuild/waves/3dk/recovery-3dk.md`.
